title: Lab 6
text:
This lab accompanies the Week 6 notes, Data Visualisation Principles.

Be able to map variables from data frames to aesthetics in ggplot2.
Use common geometries (points, lines, bars, histograms and box plots).
Use scales and coordinates, for example to zoom in on part of a plot or use a log scale.
Summarise data before plotting to reveal patterns, such as trends hidden by seasonal variation.
Recognise and avoid misleading plots.

When you have finished the lab, there are more questions on the same data in lab_06_practice.qmd, including themes, facets, colourblind-safe palettes and violin plots.


The file data/MET Office Weather Data.csv contains monthly weather observations from 36 stations in the UK between 1853 and 2020. The fields included are:

year: Year in which the measurements were taken
month: Month in which the measurements were taken
tmax: Mean daily maximum temperature (°C)
tmin: Mean daily minimum temperature (°C)
af: Days of air frost recorded that month (days)
rain: Total rainfall (mm)
sun: Total sunshine duration (hours)
station: Station location where measurement was recorded

The year and month are stored as integers. The first cell below reads the data and adds a new column called date using the lubridate make_date function.

library(tidyverse)

Warning: package 'dplyr' was built under R version 4.4.3

met <- read_csv("data/MET Office Weather Data.csv")
met <- met |>
    mutate(date = make_date(year, month, 1))


Produce a line plot showing how the maximum temperature in July recorded in the station in Southampton has changed over time. Add nice labels to your plot.
There appears to be a break in the plotted line. Work out where it is by using coord_cartesian to zoom in on the \(x\) axis, and then check the dataset to identify the root cause. (Hint: look at the xlim argument of coord_cartesian. The \(x\) axis shows dates, so the limits need to be dates too.)


Solution. Below, find the plot.

met |>
    filter(station == "southampton" & month == 7) |>
    ggplot(aes(x = date, y = tmax)) +
    geom_line() +
    labs(
        x = "Date",
        y = "Maximum temperature (°C)",
        title = "July maximum temperatures in Southampton"
    )








In the full plot there is a short gap in the line just after 1940, but it is hard to see exactly where it starts and ends. Zooming in on the \(x\) axis to 1925–1950 makes it much clearer:

met |>
    filter(station == "southampton" & month == 7) |>
    ggplot(aes(x = date, y = tmax)) +
    geom_line() +
    labs(
        x = "Date",
        y = "Maximum temperature (°C)",
        title = "July maximum temperatures in Southampton"
    ) +
    coord_cartesian(xlim = c(ymd("1925-01-01"), ymd("1950-12-31")))








The gap lies between 1940 and 1945, so we can filter the dataset to just those years to see the root cause:

met |> filter(station == "southampton" & month == 7 & year >= 1940 & year <= 1945)

# A tibble: 6 × 9
   year month  tmax  tmin    af  rain   sun station     date      
  <dbl> <dbl> <dbl> <dbl> <dbl> <dbl> <dbl> <chr>       <date>    
1  1940     7  20.2  11.7     0  98.3  208  southampton 1940-07-01
2  1941     7  NA    13.2     0  47.2  239. southampton 1941-07-01
3  1942     7  20.7  11.9     0  45    173  southampton 1942-07-01
4  1943     7  22.1  12.6     0  53.6  208. southampton 1943-07-01
5  1944     7  20.9  13.4     0  68.8  119. southampton 1944-07-01
6  1945     7  21.8  12.8     0  56.1  214. southampton 1945-07-01


The break is due to an NA value of tmax in 1941: the row for July 1941 exists, but the maximum temperature was not recorded. geom_line cannot draw a line to a missing value, so it leaves a gap, rather than joining 1940 directly to 1942.

Next we look at every month of the year, not just July, at four stations.

Produce a scatter plot of the maximum temperature tmax against date for every month in Southampton, Oxford, Sheffield and Paisley. Colour the points by station.
Look up the function geom_smooth. Use the function to overlay a smooth trend line on the points. Make sure the line is visible by adjusting the alpha property on geom_point.
What does the line tell you about the trend of historical maximum temperatures?


Solution. The next plot shows a scatter plot by station:

stations <- c("southampton", "oxford", "sheffield", "paisley")
met |>
    filter(station %in% stations) |>
    ggplot(aes(x = date, y = tmax, colour = station)) +
    geom_point(alpha = 0.2) +
    geom_smooth() +
    labs(
        x = "Date",
        y = "Maximum temperature (°C)",
        title = "Monthly maximum temperatures"
    )

`geom_smooth()` using method = 'gam' and formula = 'y ~ s(x, bs = "cs")'


Warning: Removed 172 rows containing non-finite outside the scale range
(`stat_smooth()`).


Warning: Removed 172 rows containing missing values or values outside the scale range
(`geom_point()`).









geom_smooth() prints a message saying which method it used. Unlike the straight method = "lm" lines in the Week 6 notes, here it has fitted a flexible curve (method = 'gam'), which can bend to follow the data. The grey band around each line shows the uncertainty in the fitted curve (a confidence interval); it is narrow here because there is a lot of data. Lowering alpha makes the individual points faint, so the lines stand out.
The smooth lines rise slightly at each station, which hints at an increasing trend. But it is hard to be sure from this plot. Because every month of the year is included, the points at each station span a band about 20°C tall (cold winters to warm summers), and any long-term change is small by comparison.

The plot above mixes together every month of the year, so the seasonal cycle hides the long-term trend. Averaging over each year removes the seasonal cycle, since every (complete) year contains one of each month.

For each of Southampton, Oxford, Sheffield and Paisley, compute the mean tmax in each year. Plot these annual means against year as a line plot, coloured by station, and add a smooth trend line. Is the trend easier to see now?
Some of the annual means look suspicious. Which years have the lowest and highest annual means? How many months of data is each annual mean based on? (Hint: how would you count the non-missing values of a column inside summarise?)
Redraw the plot using only years with a complete set of 12 months. Roughly how much have annual mean maximum temperatures risen at these stations?


Solution. We compute the annual means, and also count how many months of tmax each mean is based on, since we will need this below:

annual <- met |>
    filter(station %in% stations) |>
    group_by(station, year) |>
    summarise(
        mean_tmax = mean(tmax, na.rm = TRUE),
        n_months = sum(!is.na(tmax)),
        .groups = "drop"
    )

annual |>
    ggplot(aes(x = year, y = mean_tmax, colour = station)) +
    geom_line() +
    geom_smooth() +
    labs(
        x = "Year",
        y = "Annual mean maximum temperature (°C)",
        title = "Annual mean maximum temperatures"
    )

`geom_smooth()` using method = 'loess' and formula = 'y ~ x'


Warning: Removed 11 rows containing non-finite outside the scale range
(`stat_smooth()`).


Warning: Removed 10 rows containing missing values or values outside the scale range
(`geom_line()`).









The \(y\) axis now covers a few degrees rather than 25, and the upward trend is much easier to see. But there are some odd spikes, particularly at the ends of the records. Sorting by mean_tmax shows the most extreme years:

annual |> arrange(mean_tmax) |> head(5)

# A tibble: 5 × 4
  station      year mean_tmax n_months
  <chr>       <dbl>     <dbl>    <int>
1 paisley      2011       7.9        3
2 sheffield    1923      10.6        6
3 southampton  2000      10.8        3
4 oxford       1879      10.9       12
5 sheffield    1892      11.3       12

annual |> arrange(desc(mean_tmax)) |> head(5)

# A tibble: 5 × 4
  station      year mean_tmax n_months
  <chr>       <dbl>     <dbl>    <int>
1 oxford       2019      16.8        5
2 southampton  1959      16.4       12
3 southampton  1949      16.4       12
4 southampton  1995      16.0       12
5 southampton  1921      16.0       12


The coldest “year” in the data is Paisley in 2011, but that mean is based on only 3 months of data; the warmest is Oxford in 2019, based on only 5 months. An annual mean from a partial year depends on which months are present: a year containing only winter months will look very cold. Using na.rm = TRUE made the mean calculation work, but it did not make the answer meaningful. (Where a station has no tmax values at all for a year, mean(..., na.rm = TRUE) returns NaN, “not a number”, and ggplot drops these rows with a warning.)
Keeping only complete years:

annual |>
    filter(n_months == 12) |>
    ggplot(aes(x = year, y = mean_tmax, colour = station)) +
    geom_line() +
    geom_smooth() +
    labs(
        x = "Year",
        y = "Annual mean maximum temperature (°C)",
        title = "Annual mean maximum temperatures (complete years only)"
    )

`geom_smooth()` using method = 'loess' and formula = 'y ~ x'









Oxford and Sheffield warm by about 2°C over their records, most of it since around 1980. Southampton warms by about 1°C, more steadily, although its record stops in 2000. Paisley’s record is too short (1959–2011) to say much on its own. Note that when we filter out incomplete years, geom_line simply joins the remaining points, so there is no break in the line where a year is missing. Compare this with the July plot at the start of this task, where an NA value produced a visible gap.





Produce a bar chart showing how many monthly records there are for each station, using geom_bar(). Then produce the same chart using count() and geom_col(). (Hint: to make the station names readable, add theme(axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 45, hjust = 1)) to your plot.)


Solution. geom_bar() counts the rows in each category for us, so we only need to give it an x aesthetic.

met |>
    ggplot(aes(x = station)) +
    geom_bar() +
    labs(
        x = "Station",
        y = "Number of monthly records",
        title = "Number of monthly records by station"
    ) +
    theme(axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 45, hjust = 1))








Alternatively we can count the rows ourselves with count(), which creates a column n. The bar heights are then already in the data, so we use geom_col():

met |>
    count(station) |>
    ggplot(aes(x = station, y = n)) +
    geom_col() +
    labs(
        x = "Station",
        y = "Number of monthly records",
        title = "Number of monthly records by station"
    ) +
    theme(axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 45, hjust = 1))








The two plots are identical.


Produce a bar chart showing the average rainfall (across all months and years) for the 5 stations with the highest average rainfall.
Now make a deliberately misleading version of this plot, which suggests that Cwmystwyth gets several times as much rain as Stornoway. Which of the principles in the Week 6 notes does your plot break? How could a reader spot the trick?


Solution. We first compute the mean rainfall at each station with group_by and summarise. Because we have already computed the height of each bar, we use geom_col(); geom_bar() would instead count the rows in each category. To keep only the five wettest stations, we sort the summarised data with arrange(desc(...)) and keep the first five rows with head(5) before passing it to ggplot.

met |>
    group_by(station) |>
    summarise(mean_rainfall = mean(rain, na.rm = TRUE), .groups = "drop") |>
    arrange(desc(mean_rainfall)) |>
    head(5) |>
    ggplot(aes(x = station, y = mean_rainfall)) +
    geom_col() +
    labs(
        x = "Station",
        y = "Mean monthly rainfall (mm)",
        title = "Mean monthly rainfall at the five wettest stations"
    ) +
    theme(axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 45, hjust = 1))








Cwmystwyth has a mean monthly rainfall of about 150 mm and Stornoway about 100 mm, so Cwmystwyth is only about 1.5 times as wet. To make the difference look much bigger, we can zoom in on the \(y\) axis with coord_cartesian, as we did in Task 1, so that the bars no longer start at zero:

met |>
    group_by(station) |>
    summarise(mean_rainfall = mean(rain, na.rm = TRUE), .groups = "drop") |>
    arrange(desc(mean_rainfall)) |>
    head(5) |>
    ggplot(aes(x = station, y = mean_rainfall)) +
    geom_col() +
    coord_cartesian(ylim = c(95, 150)) +
    labs(
        x = "Station",
        y = "Mean monthly rainfall (mm)",
        title = "Mean monthly rainfall at the five wettest stations"
    ) +
    theme(axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 45, hjust = 1))








The Cwmystwyth bar is now around seven times as tall as the Stornoway bar. This breaks the first principle, “Be honest with scales”: we read a bar chart by comparing the lengths of the bars, so the value axis should start at zero. It is the same trick as the welfare chart in the Week 6 notes. Nothing in the plot is technically false: a careful reader can spot the trick by checking where the \(y\) axis starts. But most readers will judge the bar lengths rather than read the axis.
(Setting scale_y_continuous(limits = c(95, 150)) instead does not work: ggplot removes any bar that extends outside the scale limits, and since every bar starts at zero, all five disappear with a warning. coord_cartesian zooms in on the plot after the bars have been drawn, instead.)

Bar charts of averages hide how much the rainfall varies from month to month, so next we look at its distribution.

Look up how to produce a box plot with ggplot, and produce a box plot of rainfall at each station. Are there any outliers at the low end? Why not?


Solution. Box plots use geom_boxplot(), with the grouping variable on one axis and the numeric variable on the other.

met |>
    ggplot(aes(x = station, y = rain)) +
    geom_boxplot() +
    labs(
        x = "Station",
        y = "Rainfall (mm)",
        title = "Distribution of monthly rainfall by station"
    ) +
    theme(axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 45, hjust = 1))

Warning: Removed 1498 rows containing non-finite outside the scale range
(`stat_boxplot()`).









By default, the whiskers extend up to 1.5 times the interquartile range (IQR) beyond the box, and any points outside them are drawn as outliers. There are plenty of high outliers (very wet months), but no low outliers at all. Rainfall cannot be negative, and at every station the lower whisker limit (the lower quartile minus 1.5 times the IQR) is below zero, so no value can fall beneath it.


Plot a histogram of monthly rainfall across all stations. Experiment with the bins argument. How would you describe the shape of the distribution?
Redraw the histogram with a logarithmic \(x\) axis (see the Week 6 notes). What happens to the shape? Read the warning messages carefully, and compare the number of rows removed with the previous histogram. Which months have been dropped, and why?


Solution. A histogram needs only an x aesthetic: geom_histogram() divides the \(x\) axis into bins and counts the rows in each one.

met |>
    ggplot(aes(x = rain)) +
    geom_histogram(bins = 50) +
    labs(
        x = "Monthly rainfall (mm)",
        y = "Number of months",
        title = "Distribution of monthly rainfall across all stations"
    )

Warning: Removed 1498 rows containing non-finite outside the scale range
(`stat_bin()`).









With too few bins (say 5) the shape is lost; with too many (say 500) the histogram becomes noisy. Something in the range 30–100 works well here.
The distribution is strongly right-skewed: half of all months have between about 40 and 95 mm of rain (the median is 63 mm), but there is a long tail of very wet months reaching up to 569 mm (Eskdalemuir, December 2015). On the left the distribution stops sharply at zero, since rainfall cannot be negative.
For the log scale, we add a scale transformation, as in the Week 6 notes:

met |>
    ggplot(aes(x = rain)) +
    geom_histogram(bins = 50) +
    scale_x_continuous(transform = "log10") +
    labs(
        x = "Monthly rainfall (mm, log scale)",
        y = "Number of months",
        title = "Distribution of monthly rainfall across all stations"
    )

Warning in scale_x_continuous(transform = "log10"): log-10 transformation
introduced infinite values.


Warning: Removed 1503 rows containing non-finite outside the scale range
(`stat_bin()`).









The log scale stretches out small values and squashes large ones. The long tail of wet months is pulled in, and the distribution is now left-skewed instead, with a tail of unusually dry months (below 10 mm). So the log scale does not make the distribution symmetric, but it does make the dry months, which were squashed against zero before, much easier to see.
There are two warnings. The first says that the log transformation “introduced infinite values”, and the second that 1503 rows were removed, compared with 1498 for the original histogram. The 1498 are the rows where rain is NA. The extra 5 are months with zero rainfall, because \(\log_{10}(0) = -\infty\) cannot be plotted:

met |> filter(rain == 0)

# A tibble: 5 × 9
   year month  tmax  tmin    af  rain   sun station     date      
  <dbl> <dbl> <dbl> <dbl> <dbl> <dbl> <dbl> <chr>       <date>    
1  1986     2   2.3  -2.7    24     0 117   aberporth   1986-02-01
2  1959     2   6.6   2       4     0  73.4 eastbourne  1959-02-01
3  1957     4  13.5   5.1     0     0 140.  rossonwye   1957-04-01
4  1925     6  22.7  10.9     0     0 327.  southampton 1925-06-01
5  1940     8  22.1  12.1     0     0 238.  southampton 1940-08-01


Some UK months really have been this dry, so these are probably genuine observations rather than errors, yet the log scale drops them from the plot. It is always worth reading warnings like this rather than ignoring them.

Compare this with the July plot at the start of this task, where an NA value produced a visible gap.





Produce a bar chart showing how many monthly records there are for each station, using geom_bar(). Then produce the same chart using count() and geom_col(). (Hint: to make the station names readable, add theme(axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 45, hjust = 1)) to your plot.)


Solution. geom_bar() counts the rows in each category for us, so we only need to give it an x aesthetic.

met |>
    ggplot(aes(x = station)) +
    geom_bar() +
    labs(
        x = "Station",
        y = "Number of monthly records",
        title = "Number of monthly records by station"
    ) +
    theme(axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 45, hjust = 1))








Alternatively we can count the rows ourselves with count(), which creates a column n. The bar heights are then already in the data, so we use geom_col():

met |>
    count(station) |>
    ggplot(aes(x = station, y = n)) +
    geom_col() +
    labs(
        x = "Station",
        y = "Number of monthly records",
        title = "Number of monthly records by station"
    ) +
    theme(axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 45, hjust = 1))








The two plots are identical.


Produce a bar chart showing the average rainfall (across all months and years) for the 5 stations with the highest average rainfall.
Now make a deliberately misleading version of this plot, which suggests that Cwmystwyth gets several times as much rain as Stornoway. Which of the principles in the Week 6 notes does your plot break? How could a reader spot the trick?


Solution. We first compute the mean rainfall at each station with group_by and summarise. Because we have already computed the height of each bar, we use geom_col(); geom_bar() would instead count the rows in each category. To keep only the five wettest stations, we sort the summarised data with arrange(desc(...)) and keep the first five rows with head(5) before passing it to ggplot.

met |>
    group_by(station) |>
    summarise(mean_rainfall = mean(rain, na.rm = TRUE), .groups = "drop") |>
    arrange(desc(mean_rainfall)) |>
    head(5) |>
    ggplot(aes(x = station, y = mean_rainfall)) +
    geom_col() +
    labs(
        x = "Station",
        y = "Mean monthly rainfall (mm)",
        title = "Mean monthly rainfall at the five wettest stations"
    ) +
    theme(axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 45, hjust = 1))








Cwmystwyth has a mean monthly rainfall of about 150 mm and Stornoway about 100 mm, so Cwmystwyth is only about 1.5 times as wet. To make the difference look much bigger, we can zoom in on the \(y\) axis with coord_cartesian, as we did in Task 1, so that the bars no longer start at zero:

met |>
    group_by(station) |>
    summarise(mean_rainfall = mean(rain, na.rm = TRUE), .groups = "drop") |>
    arrange(desc(mean_rainfall)) |>
    head(5) |>
    ggplot(aes(x = station, y = mean_rainfall)) +
    geom_col() +
    coord_cartesian(ylim = c(95, 150)) +
    labs(
        x = "Station",
        y = "Mean monthly rainfall (mm)",
        title = "Mean monthly rainfall at the five wettest stations"
    ) +
    theme(axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 45, hjust = 1))








The Cwmystwyth bar is now around seven times as tall as the Stornoway bar. This breaks the first principle, “Be honest with scales”: we read a bar chart by comparing the lengths of the bars, so the value axis should start at zero. It is the same trick as the welfare chart in the Week 6 notes. Nothing in the plot is technically false: a careful reader can spot the trick by checking where the \(y\) axis starts. But most readers will judge the bar lengths rather than read the axis.
(Setting scale_y_continuous(limits = c(95, 150)) instead does not work: ggplot removes any bar that extends outside the scale limits, and since every bar starts at zero, all five disappear with a warning. coord_cartesian zooms in on the plot after the bars have been drawn, instead.)

Bar charts of averages hide how much the rainfall varies from month to month, so next we look at its distribution.

Look up how to produce a box plot with ggplot, and produce a box plot of rainfall at each station. Are there any outliers at the low end? Why not?


Solution. Box plots use geom_boxplot(), with the grouping variable on one axis and the numeric variable on the other.

met |>
    ggplot(aes(x = station, y = rain)) +
    geom_boxplot() +
    labs(
        x = "Station",
        y = "Rainfall (mm)",
        title = "Distribution of monthly rainfall by station"
    ) +
    theme(axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 45, hjust = 1))

Warning: Removed 1498 rows containing non-finite outside the scale range
(`stat_boxplot()`).









By default, the whiskers extend up to 1.5 times the interquartile range (IQR) beyond the box, and any points outside them are drawn as outliers. There are plenty of high outliers (very wet months), but no low outliers at all. Rainfall cannot be negative, and at every station the lower whisker limit (the lower quartile minus 1.5 times the IQR) is below zero, so no value can fall beneath it.


Plot a histogram of monthly rainfall across all stations. Experiment with the bins argument. How would you describe the shape of the distribution?
Redraw the histogram with a logarithmic \(x\) axis (see the Week 6 notes). What happens to the shape? Read the warning messages carefully, and compare the number of rows removed with the previous histogram. Which months have been dropped, and why?


Solution. A histogram needs only an x aesthetic: geom_histogram() divides the \(x\) axis into bins and counts the rows in each one.

met |>
    ggplot(aes(x = rain)) +
    geom_histogram(bins = 50) +
    labs(
        x = "Monthly rainfall (mm)",
        y = "Number of months",
        title = "Distribution of monthly rainfall across all stations"
    )

Warning: Removed 1498 rows containing non-finite outside the scale range
(`stat_bin()`).









With too few bins (say 5) the shape is lost; with too many (say 500) the histogram becomes noisy. Something in the range 30–100 works well here.
The distribution is strongly right-skewed: half of all months have between about 40 and 95 mm of rain (the median is 63 mm), but there is a long tail of very wet months reaching up to 569 mm (Eskdalemuir, December 2015). On the left the distribution stops sharply at zero, since rainfall cannot be negative.
For the log scale, we add a scale transformation, as in the Week 6 notes:

met |>
    ggplot(aes(x = rain)) +
    geom_histogram(bins = 50) +
    scale_x_continuous(transform = "log10") +
    labs(
        x = "Monthly rainfall (mm, log scale)",
        y = "Number of months",
        title = "Distribution of monthly rainfall across all stations"
    )

Warning in scale_x_continuous(transform = "log10"): log-10 transformation
introduced infinite values.


Warning: Removed 1503 rows containing non-finite outside the scale range
(`stat_bin()`).









The log scale stretches out small values and squashes large ones. The long tail of wet months is pulled in, and the distribution is now left-skewed instead, with a tail of unusually dry months (below 10 mm). So the log scale does not make the distribution symmetric, but it does make the dry months, which were squashed against zero before, much easier to see.
There are two warnings. The first says that the log transformation “introduced infinite values”, and the second that 1503 rows were removed, compared with 1498 for the original histogram. The 1498 are the rows where rain is NA. The extra 5 are months with zero rainfall, because \(\log_{10}(0) = -\infty\) cannot be plotted:

met |> filter(rain == 0)

# A tibble: 5 × 9
   year month  tmax  tmin    af  rain   sun station     date      
  <dbl> <dbl> <dbl> <dbl> <dbl> <dbl> <dbl> <chr>       <date>    
1  1986     2   2.3  -2.7    24     0 117   aberporth   1986-02-01
2  1959     2   6.6   2       4     0  73.4 eastbourne  1959-02-01
3  1957     4  13.5   5.1     0     0 140.  rossonwye   1957-04-01
4  1925     6  22.7  10.9     0     0 327.  southampton 1925-06-01
5  1940     8  22.1  12.1     0     0 238.  southampton 1940-08-01


Some UK months really have been this dry, so these are probably genuine observations rather than errors, yet the log scale drops them from the plot. It is always worth reading warnings like this rather than ignoring them.

title: Lab 8 Practice Questions
text:
These questions are for extra practice after Lab 8. Tasks 1 and 2 follow on from Task 1 of the lab, and use the app in src/samples.R. Tasks 3–7 follow on from Task 2 of the lab, and build on your visualiser of the penguins data (Task 5 also uses ideas from Task 1). As in the lab, write your Shiny apps in the src/ subdirectory, and your answers to the questions in this document. Questions marked Extension are more challenging, and the question marked Challenge is much harder still.


This task follows on from Task 1 of the lab.
The file src/samples.R contains the app from the Reactive Expressions section of the Week 8 notes, with two changes: it draws a sample of only 10 points, and it also displays them in a table.

Run the app and change \(\mu_1\) a few times. Check that the plot, the sample means and the table all describe the same points.
Copy src/samples.R to a new file, src/samples_no_reactive.R. In the copy, remove the reactive expression samples() from the server: instead, draw the sample inside each of the three render* functions. Run the new app. What has gone wrong?
Explain what you have seen, using the reactive graph of each version of the app.
Suppose you tried to fix the problem by calling set.seed(1) at the start of each render* function. Would the outputs agree? Why is a reactive expression still the better solution?


Solution. The app without the reactive expression is in solutions/samples_no_reactive.R. Each output now draws its own sample of 10 points, so the plot, the printed means and the table describe three different samples: the points in the table are not the points in the plot, and the printed means are not the means of either.
In the original app, the reactive graph has the two inputs as sources, samples() as a conductor, and the three outputs as endpoints that all read samples(). When \(\mu_1\) changes, samples() is recomputed once, and all three outputs read that same, cached sample. Without the conductor, each input is connected directly to each of the three endpoints, and each endpoint calls rnorm for itself. Nothing in the graph says that the three outputs should share their data, so they don’t.
Calling set.seed(1) at the start of each render* function does make the outputs agree: each one resets the random number generator to the same state, then draws the same numbers in the same order, so all three generate the same sample. (As the notes point out, changing \(\mu_1\) then slides the same cloud of points left or right, rather than drawing a new one.) But this is a fragile fix:

The sampling code is copied three times, and the copies must stay exactly the same. Change the sample size, or swap the order of the two rnorm calls, in one copy but not the others, and the outputs silently disagree again.
The sample is computed three times instead of once.

A reactive expression guarantees that every output uses the same sample, and the code that draws it is written only once.




This task follows on from Task 1 of the lab, and uses the app in src/samples.R from Task 1 above.
At the moment, the app draws a new sample every time \(\mu_1\) or \(\mu_2\) changes, so the points jump around as well as moving.

Copy src/samples.R to a new file, src/resample.R. Change the copy so that changing \(\mu_1\) or \(\mu_2\) moves the same points, and a new sample is drawn only when the user presses a “Draw a new sample” button. Use an actionButton, observeEvent and a reactiveVal. (Hint: if z is drawn with rnorm(10), then mu + z is a sample with mean mu and standard deviation 1.)
Sketch the reactive graph of your new app. What re-runs when the user changes \(\mu_1\)? What re-runs when they press the button?
Your reactiveVal probably holds the standard normal sample (z), not the sample that is plotted. Why would it be a bad idea to store the plotted sample in the reactiveVal instead?


Solution. A solution is in solutions/resample.R. Its server stores a standard normal sample in a reactiveVal, replaces it in an observeEvent each time the button is pressed, and adds \(\mu_1\) and \(\mu_2\) to it in the reactive expression samples():
noise <- reactiveVal(tibble(z1 = rnorm(10), z2 = rnorm(10)))

observeEvent(input$resample, {
  noise(tibble(z1 = rnorm(10), z2 = rnorm(10)))
})

samples <- reactive(tibble(
  x1 = input$mu1 + noise()$z1,
  x2 = input$mu2 + noise()$z2
))
The rest of the server is unchanged: the three outputs still read samples(). This follows the rule of thumb in the notes. Pressing the button should make something happen, drawing new random numbers, so it is handled by an observer. The noise is a value that only the server changes, so it is stored in a reactiveVal. The plotted sample is a value computed from other reactive values, so it is a reactive expression.
In the reactive graph, the sources are input$mu1, input$mu2, input$resample and noise; the conductor is samples(), which reads input$mu1, input$mu2 and noise(); and the endpoints are the observer, which reads only input$resample, and the three outputs, which read samples().

Changing \(\mu_1\) invalidates samples(), so it is recomputed (once) and all three outputs re-run. noise has not changed, so every point moves by the same amount in the \(x\) direction.
Pressing the button runs the observer, which sets noise to a new sample. That invalidates samples(), and so the three outputs re-run with new points. The observer is the only thing that reads input$resample.

To store the plotted sample in the reactiveVal instead, observers would have to update it when \(\mu_1\) or \(\mu_2\) changes, as well as when the button is pressed. Redrawing the sample each time brings back the jumping points we were trying to remove, while shifting the existing points means remembering the old values of \(\mu_1\) and \(\mu_2\) to work out how far to move them. Either way, it is what the notes warn against: using an observer to compute a value and store it in a reactiveVal, when a reactive expression does the job more simply.




This task follows on from Task 2 of the lab.

Extension: Change your visualiser so that the user can choose which categorical variable to filter on, as well as the value to keep. Hint: the values to choose from depend on the variable, so build that dropdown in the server with renderUI, as in Task 1 of the lab. .data[[...]] works inside dplyr functions such as filter() in the same way as in aes():

library(tidyverse)
# Run in the console, from the project folder
penguins <- read_csv("src/data/penguins.csv")
col <- "species"
penguins |> filter(.data[[col]] == "Adelie")

Solution. A solution is in solutions/datavis_extension.R. In place of the species dropdown, the ui has a selectInput called filter_var for the variable, and a uiOutput for the dropdown of values, which the server builds from the chosen column:
output$filter_value_ui <- renderUI({
  values <- sort(unique(na.omit(penguins[[input$filter_var]])))
  selectInput("filter_value", "Show only:", choices = c("(All)" = "", values))
})

selected <- reactive({
  if (isTRUE(input$filter_value %in% penguins[[input$filter_var]])) {
    penguins |>
      filter(.data[[input$filter_var]] == input$filter_value)
  } else {
    penguins
  }
})
The test in selected() is the subtle part. input$filter_value is NULL until the dropdown first appears, and just after the user chooses a new filter variable it still holds a value of the old one (say "Dream" while filtering by sex), until the new dropdown has been sent to the browser. Filtering on "Dream" in the sex column would briefly leave no rows at all, so the plot would flash up empty. Only filtering on a value that belongs to the current variable avoids this: in every other case (including "(All)", whose value is ""), the whole dataset is shown.




This task follows on from Task 2 of the lab, and uses your visualiser.

Use your visualiser to find the pair of measurements that best separates the three species. How confident are you in your answer, and what could mislead you?
Colour the points by sex. What are the grey points, and how many are there? Should your app show them? Change it to handle them in the way you think is best.


Solution. Any plot with bill length on one axis separates the species into three clusters that hardly overlap; bill length against bill depth is the clearest. Bill length separates Adelie penguins (a mean of 38.8 mm) from the other two species (47.5 mm and 48.8 mm), and bill depth separates Gentoo penguins (15.0 mm) from Chinstraps (18.4 mm). Without bill length, Adelie and Chinstrap penguins overlap almost completely: their mean bill depths (18.3 and 18.4 mm), flipper lengths (190 and 196 mm) and body masses (3,701 and 3,733 g) are all very close.
We should be fairly, but not completely, confident:

A few penguins sit between the clusters, so “best” is a judgement made by eye.
Species and island are confounded: Chinstraps were only measured on Dream, and Gentoos only on Biscoe, so some of the difference between species could be a difference between islands. Adelie penguins were measured on all three islands, and filtering to them shows that their measurements barely differ between islands, which suggests that island is not the explanation.
Males are larger than females (for example, male Gentoos are about 800 g heavier than females), which spreads out each species’ cluster, and the groups are of different sizes (only 68 Chinstraps).
If the axes are not fixed, as in Task 2 of the lab, plots of single species can mislead.

The grey points are penguins whose sex is missing (NA), which ggplot2 draws in grey and labels NA in the legend. The sex of 11 penguins is missing, but only 9 grey points appear (5 Adelie and 4 Gentoo): the other 2 penguins have no measurements at all, so are never plotted.
There is no single right answer to whether to show them. They are genuine measurements, so removing those penguins from every plot would throw away data; but NA is not a sex, and a legend entry for it may confuse a user. One reasonable choice is to leave out the penguins whose value of the colour variable is missing, which only affects the plot when colouring by sex, by filtering inside renderPlot before plotting:
plot_data <- selected() |>
  filter(!is.na(.data[[input$colour_var]]))
and then plotting plot_data rather than selected(). Whatever you choose, it is good practice to tell the user, for example in a caption added with labs(caption = ...), that some penguins are not shown.




This task combines ideas from both tasks of the lab.

Sketch the reactive graph of your visualiser from Task 2 of the lab, as you did for your first app in Task 1 of the lab.
What re-runs when the user types a title? What re-runs when they choose a species? Is the data filtered again when the title changes?


Solution. In the model solution (solutions/datavis.R), the sources are the seven inputs; the only conductor is selected(), which reads input$species; and the only endpoint is output$plot, which reads selected() and the other six inputs.





flowchart LR
  species["input$species"] --> selected["selected()"]
  selected --> plot["output$plot"]
  x_var["input$x_var"] --> plot
  y_var["input$y_var"] --> plot
  colour_var["input$colour_var"] --> plot
  x_label["input$x_label"] --> plot
  y_label["input$y_label"] --> plot
  title["input$title"] --> plot






Typing a title re-runs only output$plot. selected() does not read the title, so it is not out of date, and the plot uses its cached result: the data is not filtered again. Choosing a species invalidates selected(), so it is recomputed, and then the plot is redrawn.
If we had filtered the data inside renderPlot instead, it would be filtered again every time a label changed. With 344 penguins that makes no visible difference, but with a large dataset or a slow calculation it would make the app sluggish.




This task follows on from Task 2 of the lab.
Deploy your visualiser (or your app from Task 1 of the lab) to shinyapps.io:

Create a “Free” tier account
In RStudio go to Tools > Global Options > Publishing.
Click Connect and choose ShinyApps.io. (RStudio may require some apps to be installed).
Follow the prompts to authorize RStudio with your shinyapps.io account. (You’ll need to copy/paste a token from the website).

Once this is completed:

Open the app you want to deploy in RStudio.
Look for the Publish button (blue icon) in the upper-right corner of the editor pane.
Click it and select Publish Application.
Choose which files to include. Make sure you include data/penguins.csv: the deployed app runs from the same folder layout, which is another reason to read the data with a path relative to the app’s own folder.
Click Publish and wait for the deployment to complete.
RStudio will automatically open your deployed app in a browser.

Then share your published app with someone! As the Limitations section of the Week 8 notes points out, anyone with the link can use your app and see the data it displays. That is fine for penguins, but think carefully before deploying an app that shows personal data.



This task follows on from Task 2 of the lab.

Challenge: This goes well beyond the Week 8 notes. Modify your visualiser from Task 2 of the lab so that the user can upload a CSV file of their own, rather than the app always using penguins.csv. (Hint: look up fileInput.) There needs to be much more dynamic server-side logic in this case: for example, the choices in every dropdown depend on the columns of the uploaded file.

No solution is provided for this task. It is really quite challenging, bringing together everything from both lab tasks along with several new ideas, and I would never expect you to do something so difficult in an assessment. It is here as a challenge if you want to see how far you can take an app.
