This task follows on from Task 2 of the lab, and uses your visualiser.

Use your visualiser to find the pair of measurements that best separates the three species. How confident are you in your answer, and what could mislead you?
Colour the points by sex. What are the grey points, and how many are there? Should your app show them? Change it to handle them in the way you think is best.


Solution. Any plot with bill length on one axis separates the species into three clusters that hardly overlap; bill length against bill depth is the clearest. Bill length separates Adelie penguins (a mean of 38.8 mm) from the other two species (47.5 mm and 48.8 mm), and bill depth separates Gentoo penguins (15.0 mm) from Chinstraps (18.4 mm). Without bill length, Adelie and Chinstrap penguins overlap almost completely: their mean bill depths (18.3 and 18.4 mm), flipper lengths (190 and 196 mm) and body masses (3,701 and 3,733 g) are all very close.
We should be fairly, but not completely, confident:

A few penguins sit between the clusters, so “best” is a judgement made by eye.
Species and island are confounded: Chinstraps were only measured on Dream, and Gentoos only on Biscoe, so some of the difference between species could be a difference between islands. Adelie penguins were measured on all three islands, and filtering to them shows that their measurements barely differ between islands, which suggests that island is not the explanation.
Males are larger than females (for example, male Gentoos are about 800 g heavier than females), which spreads out each species’ cluster, and the groups are of different sizes (only 68 Chinstraps).
If the axes are not fixed, as in Task 2 of the lab, plots of single species can mislead.

The grey points are penguins whose sex is missing (NA), which ggplot2 draws in grey and labels NA in the legend. The sex of 11 penguins is missing, but only 9 grey points appear (5 Adelie and 4 Gentoo): the other 2 penguins have no measurements at all, so are never plotted.
There is no single right answer to whether to show them. They are genuine measurements, so removing those penguins from every plot would throw away data; but NA is not a sex, and a legend entry for it may confuse a user. One reasonable choice is to leave out the penguins whose value of the colour variable is missing, which only affects the plot when colouring by sex, by filtering inside renderPlot before plotting:
plot_data <- selected() |>
  filter(!is.na(.data[[input$colour_var]]))
and then plotting plot_data rather than selected(). Whatever you choose, it is good practice to tell the user, for example in a caption added with labs(caption = ...), that some penguins are not shown.




This task combines ideas from both tasks of the lab.

Sketch the reactive graph of your visualiser from Task 2 of the lab, as you did for your first app in Task 1 of the lab.
What re-runs when the user types a title? What re-runs when they choose a species? Is the data filtered again when the title changes?


Solution. In the model solution (solutions/datavis.R), the sources are the seven inputs; the only conductor is selected(), which reads input$species; and the only endpoint is output$plot, which reads selected() and the other six inputs.





flowchart LR
  species["input$species"] --> selected["selected()"]
  selected --> plot["output$plot"]
  x_var["input$x_var"] --> plot
  y_var["input$y_var"] --> plot
  colour_var["input$colour_var"] --> plot
  x_label["input$x_label"] --> plot
  y_label["input$y_label"] --> plot
  title["input$title"] --> plot






Typing a title re-runs only output$plot. selected() does not read the title, so it is not out of date, and the plot uses its cached result: the data is not filtered again. Choosing a species invalidates selected(), so it is recomputed, and then the plot is redrawn.
If we had filtered the data inside renderPlot instead, it would be filtered again every time a label changed. With 344 penguins that makes no visible difference, but with a large dataset or a slow calculation it would make the app sluggish.




This task follows on from Task 2 of the lab.
Deploy your visualiser (or your app from Task 1 of the lab) to shinyapps.io:

Create a “Free” tier account
In RStudio go to Tools > Global Options > Publishing.
Click Connect and choose ShinyApps.io. (RStudio may require some apps to be installed).
Follow the prompts to authorize RStudio with your shinyapps.io account. (You’ll need to copy/paste a token from the website).

Once this is completed:

Open the app you want to deploy in RStudio.
Look for the Publish button (blue icon) in the upper-right corner of the editor pane.
Click it and select Publish Application.
Choose which files to include. Make sure you include data/penguins.csv: the deployed app runs from the same folder layout, which is another reason to read the data with a path relative to the app’s own folder.
Click Publish and wait for the deployment to complete.
RStudio will automatically open your deployed app in a browser.

Then share your published app with someone! As the Limitations section of the Week 8 notes points out, anyone with the link can use your app and see the data it displays. That is fine for penguins, but think carefully before deploying an app that shows personal data.



This task follows on from Task 2 of the lab.

Challenge: This goes well beyond the Week 8 notes. Modify your visualiser from Task 2 of the lab so that the user can upload a CSV file of their own, rather than the app always using penguins.csv. (Hint: look up fileInput.) There needs to be much more dynamic server-side logic in this case: for example, the choices in every dropdown depend on the columns of the uploaded file.

No solution is provided for this task. It is really quite challenging, bringing together everything from both lab tasks along with several new ideas, and I would never expect you to do something so difficult in an assessment. It is here as a challenge if you want to see how far you can take an app.

title: Lab 9 Practice Questions
text:
These questions are for extra practice after Lab 9, using the same data. Tasks 1–4 follow on from Task 1 of the lab (from loops to maps), and Tasks 5–8 from Task 2 of the lab (many files, and failing well). Questions marked Extension are more challenging.
The cell below loads the penguins data, and recreates the objects from the lab that these questions use: numbers, the combined data from the files in data/penguins split into one tibble per file, and the final version of fit_bill_model(), which checks its input.

library(tidyverse)

Warning: package 'dplyr' was built under R version 4.4.3

penguins <- read_csv("data/penguins.csv")

numbers <- 1:10

files <- list.files("data/penguins", pattern = "\\.csv$", full.names = TRUE)
penguins_all <- files |>
    set_names() |>
    map(read_csv) |>
    list_rbind(names_to = "file")
by_file <- split(penguins_all, penguins_all$file)

fit_bill_model <- function(data) {
    n_complete <- sum(!is.na(data$bill_length_mm) & !is.na(data$bill_depth_mm))
    if (n_complete < 2) {
        stop("Need at least 2 penguins with both bill measurements, but found ", n_complete, ".")
    }
    model <- lm(bill_depth_mm ~ bill_length_mm, data = data)
    tibble(
        slope = coef(model)[["bill_length_mm"]],
        intercept = coef(model)[["(Intercept)"]]
    )
}



This task follows on from Task 1 of the lab.

set.seed(123)
people <- c("Alice", "Bob", "Charlie")
greetings <- c("Hello", "Hi", "Howdy")
tibbles <- list(
    df1 = tibble(x = 1:3, y = 5:7),
    df2 = tibble(a = rnorm(5), b = rnorm(5, mean = 1)),
    df3 = penguins
)
file_names <- c("numbers", "random", "penguins")


For each number in numbers, create a logical vector that is TRUE where the number is even and FALSE where it is odd.
For each number <n> in numbers, create a string that says “Value: ”.


Solution. For each number in numbers, create a logical vector that is TRUE where the number is even and FALSE where it is odd. A number is even if its remainder on division by 2 is zero. The comparison n %% 2 == 0 is already TRUE or FALSE, so there is no need to wrap it in if_else(n %% 2 == 0, TRUE, FALSE):

evens <- map_lgl(numbers, \(n) n %% 2 == 0)
evens

 [1] FALSE  TRUE FALSE  TRUE FALSE  TRUE FALSE  TRUE FALSE  TRUE


For each number <n> in numbers, create a string that says “Value: ”.

values <- map_chr(numbers, ~ paste0("Value: ", .x))
values

 [1] "Value: 1"  "Value: 2"  "Value: 3"  "Value: 4"  "Value: 5"  "Value: 6" 
 [7] "Value: 7"  "Value: 8"  "Value: 9"  "Value: 10"




Rewrite your answers to the last two questions without using map. Why is map unnecessary here, when it was needed to calculate the mean of each vector in list_of_vectors in the lab?


Solution. 

identical(numbers %% 2 == 0, evens)

[1] TRUE

identical(paste0("Value: ", numbers), values)

[1] TRUE


%%, == and paste0() are all vectorised: given a vector, they work on every element at once, and return a vector of results. So mapping them over numbers one element at a time only adds code. mean() is different: given a list of vectors, it can’t compute the mean of each one, so in the lab we needed map to apply it to each vector in turn. As the Week 9 notes say, mapping is for functions that work on one element at a time.


For each <name> in people and each <greeting> in greetings, create a string that says <greeting> <name>.
Write each tibble in tibbles to a file with the corresponding name in file_names in the directory results/. (Hint: use the function write_csv, and look up walk2().)


Solution. For each <name> in people and each <greeting> in greetings, create a string that says <greeting> <name>. In map2, .x comes from the first vector (people) and .y from the second (greetings), so paste(.y, .x) puts the greeting first:

map2_chr(people, greetings, ~ paste(.y, .x))

[1] "Hello Alice"   "Hi Bob"        "Howdy Charlie"


Write each tibble in tibbles to a file with the corresponding name in file_names in the directory results/.
write_csv is called for its side effect of writing a file, not for the value it returns. map2 would still collect those return values (each tibble, unchanged) into a list and print it, filling the output with a page of penguins. walk2 is the version of map2 for side effects: it calls the function in the same way, then returns its input invisibly, so nothing is printed.

walk2(tibbles, file_names, ~ write_csv(.x, paste0("results/", .y, ".csv")))





This task follows on from Task 1 of the lab.

set.seed(123)
functions <- list(
    \(x) x + 1,
    \(x) x * 2,
    \(x) sqrt(x)
)

daily_returns <- rnorm(365, mean = 0.001, sd = 0.01)


Compute the sum and product of numbers.
Apply the composition of all functions in the list functions to a starting number. Hint: use the .init argument of reduce.
The daily_returns vector holds one year of daily changes in the value of an investment portfolio, as proportions: a value of 0.01 means the portfolio rose by 1% that day. Assuming all the returns are reinvested and we start with £100, calculate the portfolio value after one year.


Solution. Compute the sum and product of numbers. The operators + and * are functions of two arguments, so they can be passed to reduce like any other function; the backticks let us refer to them by name:

reduce(numbers, `+`)

[1] 55

reduce(numbers, `*`)

[1] 3628800


Apply the composition of all functions in the list functions to a starting number. Here the accumulator x is the current value, and each element f of the list is the next function to apply to it, so the functions are applied in the order of the list. Starting from 1, this gives \(1 + 1 = 2\), then \(2 \times 2 = 4\), then \(\sqrt{4} = 2\). We need .init, because the accumulator is a number while the elements of the list are functions, so the accumulator can’t start at the first element:

reduce(functions, \(x, f) f(x), .init = 1)

[1] 2


Calculate the portfolio value after one year, starting with £100.
Each day, the portfolio’s value is multiplied by 1 + r, where r is that day’s return. The accumulator is therefore the portfolio value, which is a different kind of quantity from the elements of daily_returns, so it can’t start at the first element. Instead we start it at £100 with .init:

reduce(daily_returns, \(value, r) value * (1 + r), .init = 100)

[1] 159.0491




The portfolio value after one year can also be calculated in a single line, without reduce. How? Which version would you use, and why?


Solution. The portfolio value after a year is £100 multiplied by 1 + r for every day’s return r, which is exactly what prod() computes:

value_prod <- 100 * prod(1 + daily_returns)
value_reduce <- reduce(daily_returns, \(value, r) value * (1 + r), .init = 100)
value_prod

[1] 159.0491

all.equal(value_prod, value_reduce)

[1] TRUE


(The two answers agree to within rounding error, so we compare them with all.equal() rather than ==.)
The prod() version is shorter, says what it computes more directly, and is faster, because prod() is implemented in compiled code. reduce is the tool for combining elements when there is no built-in function that does the job, such as composing the list of functions above, or, as the notes explain, when each pass through the data is expensive.


Extension: Look up the function accumulate(). Use it to calculate the value of the portfolio at the end of every day, and plot it. When was the portfolio worth least?


Solution. accumulate() works like reduce(), but returns every intermediate value of the accumulator, rather than just the last one. With .init, the first value is the starting £100, so there are 366 values: one for the start, and one for the end of each of the 365 days.

portfolio <- tibble(
    day = 0:365,
    value = accumulate(daily_returns, \(value, r) value * (1 + r), .init = 100)
)

ggplot(portfolio, aes(x = day, y = value)) +
    geom_line() +
    labs(x = "Day", y = "Portfolio value (GBP)")







portfolio |> filter(value == min(value))

# A tibble: 1 × 2
    day value
  <int> <dbl>
1     2  99.4


The portfolio was worth least at the end of the second day, just below the £100 it started with. It was below £100 on only three days (days 1, 2 and 26), and spent the rest of the year above it.




This task follows on from Task 1 of the lab, where you fitted a separate line of bill depth against bill length for each species.

Use fit_bill_model() to fit a single line to all the penguins at once, ignoring species. Compare its slope with the slopes for each species. What is going on? Draw a plot to find out. (Hint: geom_smooth(method = "lm") adds a fitted straight line to a scatter plot.)


Solution. 

fit_bill_model(penguins)

# A tibble: 1 × 2
    slope intercept
    <dbl>     <dbl>
1 -0.0850      20.9

split(penguins, penguins$species) |>
    map(fit_bill_model) |>
    list_rbind(names_to = "species")

# A tibble: 3 × 3
  species   slope intercept
  <chr>     <dbl>     <dbl>
1 Adelie    0.179     11.4 
2 Chinstrap 0.222      7.57
3 Gentoo    0.205      5.25


For every species, the slope is positive: penguins with longer bills tend to have deeper bills. But for all the penguins together, the slope is negative! A scatter plot coloured by species shows why:

ggplot(penguins, aes(x = bill_length_mm, y = bill_depth_mm)) +
    geom_point(aes(colour = species)) +
    geom_smooth(aes(colour = species), method = "lm", se = FALSE) +
    geom_smooth(method = "lm", se = FALSE, colour = "black", linetype = "dashed") +
    labs(
        x = "Bill length (mm)",
        y = "Bill depth (mm)",
        colour = "Species",
        title = "Bill depth against bill length, by species (solid) and overall (dashed)"
    )








Within each species, the line slopes upwards. But the species also differ from each other: Gentoo penguins have long but shallow bills, and Adelie penguins short but deep ones. A single line through all the penguins mostly follows these differences between the species, which run downwards, rather than the relationship within each species. This is an example of Simpson’s paradox: a trend that appears within every group can disappear, or even reverse, when the groups are combined. Fitting a separate model to each species, as in the lab, tells the more accurate story.




This task follows on from Task 1 of the lab, where you used walk for functions with side effects. Recall from the Week 9 notes that a function is pure if its result depends only on its arguments, and calling it has no side effects.

to_kg <- function(mass_g) mass_g / 1000

threshold <- 4000
is_heavy <- function(mass_g) mass_g > threshold

n_calls <- 0
count_rows <- function(data) {
    n_calls <<- n_calls + 1
    nrow(data)
}

add_noise <- function(x) x + rnorm(length(x), sd = 0.1)

drop_missing <- function(data) {
    data <- data |> filter(!is.na(body_mass_g))
    data
}

save_summary <- function(data, path) {
    result <- data |>
        summarise(n = n(), mean_mass = mean(body_mass_g, na.rm = TRUE))
    write_csv(result, path)
    result
}


Which of the functions above are pure? For each impure function, say which condition it breaks. Where you can, check your answers by experimenting.
Rewrite is_heavy so that it is pure.


Solution. 

to_kg is pure: its result depends only on mass_g, and it changes nothing.
is_heavy is impure, because its result depends on the global variable threshold as well as its argument. Changing threshold changes the answer, even though the argument is the same:


is_heavy(4500)

[1] TRUE

threshold <- 5000
is_heavy(4500)

[1] FALSE

threshold <- 4000


count_rows is impure, because it has a side effect: <<- changes the variable n_calls outside the function every time it is called. (Its result does depend only on its argument.)


count_rows(penguins)

[1] 344

count_rows(penguins)

[1] 344

n_calls

[1] 2



add_noise is impure, because it generates random numbers, so calling it twice with the same argument gives different results:


add_noise(1)

[1] 0.9790207

add_noise(1)

[1] 1.037817



drop_missing is pure, even though it seems to change its argument data. Assigning to data inside the function changes a local copy, and the tibble that was passed in is unchanged:


nrow(drop_missing(penguins))

[1] 342

nrow(penguins)

[1] 344



save_summary is impure, because writing a file is a side effect.

To make is_heavy pure, we pass the threshold in as an argument. Giving it a default value keeps calls such as is_heavy(4500) working:

is_heavy <- function(mass_g, threshold = 4000) mass_g > threshold
is_heavy(4500)

[1] TRUE

is_heavy(4500, threshold = 5000)

[1] FALSE




Extension: Rewrite save_summary as a pure function that computes the summary, and a separate step that writes it to a file. Why is this split easier to test?


Solution. 

summarise_mass <- function(data) {
    data |>
        summarise(n = n(), mean_mass = mean(body_mass_g, na.rm = TRUE))
}

mass_summary <- summarise_mass(penguins)
write_csv(mass_summary, "results/mass_summary.csv")
mass_summary

# A tibble: 1 × 2
      n mean_mass
  <int>     <dbl>
1   344     4202.


summarise_mass can now be tested by calling it on a small tibble whose answer we know, and checking what it returns, without creating any files that the test would have to read back and then tidy up. Writing the file becomes one line at the edge of the analysis, as the notes recommend: the side effects are kept few and in one place, and everything else is done by pure functions.

test_data <- tibble(body_mass_g = c(3000, 5000, NA))
stopifnot(summarise_mass(test_data)$n == 3)
stopifnot(summarise_mass(test_data)$mean_mass == 4000)





This task follows on from Task 2 of the lab, where you made fit_bill_model() check its input.

Write a function check_bill_model() that tests fit_bill_model(), in the style of check_distance() in the Week 9 notes. Include at least one test where you know the right answer, and one test that bad data are rejected with an error. (Hint: make up a tiny tibble whose points lie exactly on a line you choose.)


Solution. The points \((1, 3)\), \((2, 5)\) and \((3, 7)\) lie exactly on the line \(y = 2x + 1\), so the fitted slope must be 2 and the intercept 1. The second test uses a single complete penguin, which the lab showed is not enough to fit a line. Both test datasets are created inside the function, so that it doesn’t depend on any global variables:

check_bill_model <- function(fit_fn) {
    # points exactly on the line depth = 2 * length + 1
    on_line <- tibble(bill_length_mm = c(1, 2, 3), bill_depth_mm = c(3, 5, 7))
    result <- fit_fn(on_line)
    stopifnot(isTRUE(all.equal(result$slope, 2)))
    stopifnot(isTRUE(all.equal(result$intercept, 1)))
    # a single complete penguin is not enough to fit a line
    one_penguin <- tibble(bill_length_mm = c(40, NA), bill_depth_mm = c(18, 17))
    result <- try(fit_fn(one_penguin), silent = TRUE)
    stopifnot(inherits(result, "try-error"))
    "All tests passed."
}

check_bill_model(fit_bill_model)

[1] "All tests passed."


We compare with all.equal() rather than ==, because the fitted coefficients are not exactly 2 and 1, only very close:

on_line <- tibble(bill_length_mm = c(1, 2, 3), bill_depth_mm = c(3, 5, 7))
fit_bill_model(on_line)$intercept == 1

[1] FALSE


Writing the tests also exposes a surprise in the first version of fit_bill_model() from Task 1 of the lab, which extracted the slope with coef(model)["bill_length_mm"]. Single brackets keep the name of the element, so the slope is a named number, and all.equal() reports the difference in names, even though the values agree:

old_slope <- coef(lm(bill_depth_mm ~ bill_length_mm, data = on_line))["bill_length_mm"]
old_slope

bill_length_mm 
             2 

all.equal(old_slope, 2)

[1] "names for target but not for current"


Double brackets, [[, extract just the value, which is why the final version uses them.


Extension: Document fit_bill_model() with a roxygen comment. Then move it into a file R/models.R, and load it into your Quarto document with source().


Solution. The file R/models.R contains:
#' Fit a straight line of bill depth against bill length
#'
#' Fits a linear regression of bill depth on bill length, and returns
#' its slope and intercept.
#'
#' @param data A data frame with columns bill_length_mm and bill_depth_mm
#' @return A one-row tibble with columns slope and intercept
#' @examples
#' fit_bill_model(penguins)
fit_bill_model <- function(data) {
    n_complete <- sum(!is.na(data$bill_length_mm) & !is.na(data$bill_depth_mm))
    if (n_complete < 2) {
        stop("Need at least 2 penguins with both bill measurements, but found ", n_complete, ".")
    }
    model <- lm(bill_depth_mm ~ bill_length_mm, data = data)
    tibble(
        slope = coef(model)[["bill_length_mm"]],
        intercept = coef(model)[["(Intercept)"]]
    )
}
and the Quarto document loads it with

source("R/models.R")

The path is relative to the folder containing the Quarto document, so the project still works when it is moved to another computer.




This task follows on from Task 2 of the lab, and also uses the defensive checks from the end of it.

Write a function read_penguin_folder(path) that reads every CSV file in the folder path into a single tibble, with a column recording which file each row came from. Then try it with a misspelt folder name, such as "data/pengiuns". What happens, and why is it dangerous? Change your function so that it fails fast.


Solution. A first version just wraps the code from the lab in a function:

read_penguin_folder <- function(path) {
    list.files(path, pattern = "\\.csv$", full.names = TRUE) |>
        set_names() |>
        map(read_csv) |>
        list_rbind(names_to = "file")
}

read_penguin_folder("data/penguins") |> nrow()

[1] 344

read_penguin_folder("data/pengiuns")

data frame with 0 columns and 0 rows


With the misspelt name there is no error at all. list.files() doesn’t complain about a folder that doesn’t exist: it returns an empty vector of file names. Mapping over an empty vector gives an empty list, and list_rbind() turns that into a data frame with no rows and no columns. The problem only shows up later, when some other code looks for a column that isn’t there, far from its real cause:

read_penguin_folder("data/pengiuns") |> count(species)

Error in `count()`:
! Must group by variables found in `.data`.
✖ Column `species` is not found.


To fail fast, the function should check that it found some files before reading them:

read_penguin_folder <- function(path) {
    files <- list.files(path, pattern = "\\.csv$", full.names = TRUE)
    if (length(files) == 0) {
        stop("No CSV files found in '", path, "'. Is the folder name right?")
    }
    files |>
        set_names() |>
        map(read_csv) |>
        list_rbind(names_to = "file")
}


read_penguin_folder("data/pengiuns")

Error in read_penguin_folder("data/pengiuns"): No CSV files found in 'data/pengiuns'. Is the folder name right?






This task follows on from Task 2 of the lab, where you used possibly() to skip the files that could not be fitted.

possibly() skips failures silently. Instead, use tryCatch() to fit fit_bill_model() to each file in by_file, so that each file that can’t be fitted is skipped with a message saying which file it was and what went wrong. Combine the results for the other files into a single tibble.


Solution. The function needs to know the name of the file as well as its data, so that it can report it, so we map over both the tibbles and their names with map2. Inside the error function, conditionMessage(e) returns the error’s message: here, the clear message from our defensive fit_bill_model().

fit_or_report <- function(data, file) {
    tryCatch(
        fit_bill_model(data),
        error = function(e) {
            message("Skipping ", file, ": ", conditionMessage(e))
            NULL
        }
    )
}

file_fits <- map2(by_file, names(by_file), fit_or_report)

Skipping data/penguins/chinstrap_2008.csv: Need at least 2 penguins with both bill measurements, but found 0.

file_fits |>
    compact() |>
    list_rbind(names_to = "file")

# A tibble: 8 × 3
  file                             slope intercept
  <chr>                            <dbl>     <dbl>
1 data/penguins/adelie_2007.csv    0.167     12.3 
2 data/penguins/adelie_2008.csv    0.161     12.0 
3 data/penguins/adelie_2009.csv    0.215      9.71
4 data/penguins/chinstrap_2007.csv 0.152     11.1 
5 data/penguins/chinstrap_2009.csv 0.204      8.34
6 data/penguins/gentoo_2007.csv    0.201      5.23
7 data/penguins/gentoo_2008.csv    0.205      5.31
8 data/penguins/gentoo_2009.csv    0.195      5.84






This task follows on from Task 2 of the lab.

Using the per-file results from the lab, compare the slopes for each species across the three years. Has the relationship between bill length and bill depth changed over time for any species? What would you conclude, and how confident are you?


Solution. We fit the model to each file, as in the lab, and add the number of penguins each slope is based on:

fit_or_null <- possibly(fit_bill_model, otherwise = NULL)

slopes <- by_file |>
    map(fit_or_null) |>
    compact() |>
    list_rbind(names_to = "file")

n_complete <- by_file |>
    map_int(\(df) sum(!is.na(df$bill_length_mm) & !is.na(df$bill_depth_mm)))

slopes |>
    mutate(n = n_complete[file]) |>
    select(file, slope, n)

# A tibble: 8 × 3
  file                             slope     n
  <chr>                            <dbl> <int>
1 data/penguins/adelie_2007.csv    0.167    49
2 data/penguins/adelie_2008.csv    0.161    50
3 data/penguins/adelie_2009.csv    0.215    52
4 data/penguins/chinstrap_2007.csv 0.152    26
5 data/penguins/chinstrap_2009.csv 0.204    24
6 data/penguins/gentoo_2007.csv    0.201    34
7 data/penguins/gentoo_2008.csv    0.205    46
8 data/penguins/gentoo_2009.csv    0.195    43


The slopes do differ between years: the Chinstrap slope is 0.15 in 2007 and 0.20 in 2009, and the Adelie slope varies between 0.16 and 0.22. But each slope is estimated from only 24 to 52 penguins, so we should expect it to vary from year to year by chance, even if nothing has changed. The change in the Chinstrap slope (0.05) is no bigger than the change in the Adelie slope between 2008 and 2009, which is based on twice as many penguins, and there is no consistent direction: the Adelie and Gentoo slopes go up and down from year to year, and for Chinstraps we only have two years. So there is no convincing evidence of a change, and we should not be confident in any.
To be more definite, we would need to know how much each slope could vary by chance alone, for example from its standard error or a confidence interval, which is beyond this course. Even then, three years is a very short time over which to detect a change.

title: Lab 9 Practice Questions
text:
These questions are for extra practice after Lab 9, using the same data. Tasks 1–4 follow on from Task 1 of the lab (from loops to maps), and Tasks 5–8 from Task 2 of the lab (many files, and failing well). Questions marked Extension are more challenging.
The cell below loads the penguins data, and recreates the objects from the lab that these questions use: numbers, the combined data from the files in data/penguins split into one tibble per file, and the final version of fit_bill_model(), which checks its input.

library(tidyverse)

Warning: package 'dplyr' was built under R version 4.4.3

penguins <- read_csv("data/penguins.csv")

numbers <- 1:10

files <- list.files("data/penguins", pattern = "\\.csv$", full.names = TRUE)
penguins_all <- files |>
    set_names() |>
    map(read_csv) |>
    list_rbind(names_to = "file")
by_file <- split(penguins_all, penguins_all$file)

fit_bill_model <- function(data) {
    n_complete <- sum(!is.na(data$bill_length_mm) & !is.na(data$bill_depth_mm))
    if (n_complete < 2) {
        stop("Need at least 2 penguins with both bill measurements, but found ", n_complete, ".")
    }
    model <- lm(bill_depth_mm ~ bill_length_mm, data = data)
    tibble(
        slope = coef(model)[["bill_length_mm"]],
        intercept = coef(model)[["(Intercept)"]]
    )
}



This task follows on from Task 1 of the lab.

set.seed(123)
people <- c("Alice", "Bob", "Charlie")
greetings <- c("Hello", "Hi", "Howdy")
tibbles <- list(
    df1 = tibble(x = 1:3, y = 5:7),
    df2 = tibble(a = rnorm(5), b = rnorm(5, mean = 1)),
    df3 = penguins
)
file_names <- c("numbers", "random", "penguins")


For each number in numbers, create a logical vector that is TRUE where the number is even and FALSE where it is odd.
For each number <n> in numbers, create a string that says “Value: ”.


Solution. For each number in numbers, create a logical vector that is TRUE where the number is even and FALSE where it is odd. A number is even if its remainder on division by 2 is zero. The comparison n %% 2 == 0 is already TRUE or FALSE, so there is no need to wrap it in if_else(n %% 2 == 0, TRUE, FALSE):

evens <- map_lgl(numbers, \(n) n %% 2 == 0)
evens

 [1] FALSE  TRUE FALSE  TRUE FALSE  TRUE FALSE  TRUE FALSE  TRUE


For each number <n> in numbers, create a string that says “Value: ”.

values <- map_chr(numbers, ~ paste0("Value: ", .x))
values

 [1] "Value: 1"  "Value: 2"  "Value: 3"  "Value: 4"  "Value: 5"  "Value: 6" 
 [7] "Value: 7"  "Value: 8"  "Value: 9"  "Value: 10"




Rewrite your answers to the last two questions without using map. Why is map unnecessary here, when it was needed to calculate the mean of each vector in list_of_vectors in the lab?


Solution. 

identical(numbers %% 2 == 0, evens)

[1] TRUE

identical(paste0("Value: ", numbers), values)

[1] TRUE


%%, == and paste0() are all vectorised: given a vector, they work on every element at once, and return a vector of results. So mapping them over numbers one element at a time only adds code. mean() is different: given a list of vectors, it can’t compute the mean of each one, so in the lab we needed map to apply it to each vector in turn. As the Week 9 notes say, mapping is for functions that work on one element at a time.


For each <name> in people and each <greeting> in greetings, create a string that says <greeting> <name>.
Write each tibble in tibbles to a file with the corresponding name in file_names in the directory results/. (Hint: use the function write_csv, and look up walk2().)


Solution. For each <name> in people and each <greeting> in greetings, create a string that says <greeting> <name>. In map2, .x comes from the first vector (people) and .y from the second (greetings), so paste(.y, .x) puts the greeting first:

map2_chr(people, greetings, ~ paste(.y, .x))

[1] "Hello Alice"   "Hi Bob"        "Howdy Charlie"


Write each tibble in tibbles to a file with the corresponding name in file_names in the directory results/.
write_csv is called for its side effect of writing a file, not for the value it returns. map2 would still collect those return values (each tibble, unchanged) into a list and print it, filling the output with a page of penguins. walk2 is the version of map2 for side effects: it calls the function in the same way, then returns its input invisibly, so nothing is printed.

walk2(tibbles, file_names, ~ write_csv(.x, paste0("results/", .y, ".csv")))





This task follows on from Task 1 of the lab.

set.seed(123)
functions <- list(
    \(x) x + 1,
    \(x) x * 2,
    \(x) sqrt(x)
)

daily_returns <- rnorm(365, mean = 0.001, sd = 0.01)


Compute the sum and product of numbers.
Apply the composition of all functions in the list functions to a starting number. Hint: use the .init argument of reduce.
The daily_returns vector holds one year of daily changes in the value of an investment portfolio, as proportions: a value of 0.01 means the portfolio rose by 1% that day. Assuming all the returns are reinvested and we start with £100, calculate the portfolio value after one year.


Solution. Compute the sum and product of numbers. The operators + and * are functions of two arguments, so they can be passed to reduce like any other function; the backticks let us refer to them by name:

reduce(numbers, `+`)

[1] 55

reduce(numbers, `*`)

[1] 3628800


Apply the composition of all functions in the list functions to a starting number. Here the accumulator x is the current value, and each element f of the list is the next function to apply to it, so the functions are applied in the order of the list. Starting from 1, this gives \(1 + 1 = 2\), then \(2 \times 2 = 4\), then \(\sqrt{4} = 2\). We need .init, because the accumulator is a number while the elements of the list are functions, so the accumulator can’t start at the first element:

reduce(functions, \(x, f) f(x), .init = 1)

[1] 2


Calculate the portfolio value after one year, starting with £100.
Each day, the portfolio’s value is multiplied by 1 + r, where r is that day’s return. The accumulator is therefore the portfolio value, which is a different kind of quantity from the elements of daily_returns, so it can’t start at the first element. Instead we start it at £100 with .init:

reduce(daily_returns, \(value, r) value * (1 + r), .init = 100)

[1] 159.0491




The portfolio value after one year can also be calculated in a single line, without reduce. How? Which version would you use, and why?


Solution. The portfolio value after a year is £100 multiplied by 1 + r for every day’s return r, which is exactly what prod() computes:

value_prod <- 100 * prod(1 + daily_returns)
value_reduce <- reduce(daily_returns, \(value, r) value * (1 + r), .init = 100)
value_prod

[1] 159.0491

all.equal(value_prod, value_reduce)

[1] TRUE


(The two answers agree to within rounding error, so we compare them with all.equal() rather than ==.)
The prod() version is shorter, says what it computes more directly, and is faster, because prod() is implemented in compiled code. reduce is the tool for combining elements when there is no built-in function that does the job, such as composing the list of functions above, or, as the notes explain, when each pass through the data is expensive.


Extension: Look up the function accumulate(). Use it to calculate the value of the portfolio at the end of every day, and plot it. When was the portfolio worth least?


Solution. accumulate() works like reduce(), but returns every intermediate value of the accumulator, rather than just the last one. With .init, the first value is the starting £100, so there are 366 values: one for the start, and one for the end of each of the 365 days.

portfolio <- tibble(
    day = 0:365,
    value = accumulate(daily_returns, \(value, r) value * (1 + r), .init = 100)
)

ggplot(portfolio, aes(x = day, y = value)) +
    geom_line() +
    labs(x = "Day", y = "Portfolio value (GBP)")







portfolio |> filter(value == min(value))

# A tibble: 1 × 2
    day value
  <int> <dbl>
1     2  99.4


The portfolio was worth least at the end of the second day, just below the £100 it started with. It was below £100 on only three days (days 1, 2 and 26), and spent the rest of the year above it.




This task follows on from Task 1 of the lab, where you fitted a separate line of bill depth against bill length for each species.

Use fit_bill_model() to fit a single line to all the penguins at once, ignoring species. Compare its slope with the slopes for each species. What is going on? Draw a plot to find out. (Hint: geom_smooth(method = "lm") adds a fitted straight line to a scatter plot.)


Solution. 

fit_bill_model(penguins)

# A tibble: 1 × 2
    slope intercept
    <dbl>     <dbl>
1 -0.0850      20.9

split(penguins, penguins$species) |>
    map(fit_bill_model) |>
    list_rbind(names_to = "species")

# A tibble: 3 × 3
  species   slope intercept
  <chr>     <dbl>     <dbl>
1 Adelie    0.179     11.4 
2 Chinstrap 0.222      7.57
3 Gentoo    0.205      5.25


For every species, the slope is positive: penguins with longer bills tend to have deeper bills. But for all the penguins together, the slope is negative! A scatter plot coloured by species shows why:

ggplot(penguins, aes(x = bill_length_mm, y = bill_depth_mm)) +
    geom_point(aes(colour = species)) +
    geom_smooth(aes(colour = species), method = "lm", se = FALSE) +
    geom_smooth(method = "lm", se = FALSE, colour = "black", linetype = "dashed") +
    labs(
        x = "Bill length (mm)",
        y = "Bill depth (mm)",
        colour = "Species",
        title = "Bill depth against bill length, by species (solid) and overall (dashed)"
    )








Within each species, the line slopes upwards. But the species also differ from each other: Gentoo penguins have long but shallow bills, and Adelie penguins short but deep ones. A single line through all the penguins mostly follows these differences between the species, which run downwards, rather than the relationship within each species. This is an example of Simpson’s paradox: a trend that appears within every group can disappear, or even reverse, when the groups are combined. Fitting a separate model to each species, as in the lab, tells the more accurate story.




This task follows on from Task 1 of the lab, where you used walk for functions with side effects. Recall from the Week 9 notes that a function is pure if its result depends only on its arguments, and calling it has no side effects.

to_kg <- function(mass_g) mass_g / 1000

threshold <- 4000
is_heavy <- function(mass_g) mass_g > threshold

n_calls <- 0
count_rows <- function(data) {
    n_calls <<- n_calls + 1
    nrow(data)
}

add_noise <- function(x) x + rnorm(length(x), sd = 0.1)

drop_missing <- function(data) {
    data <- data |> filter(!is.na(body_mass_g))
    data
}

save_summary <- function(data, path) {
    result <- data |>
        summarise(n = n(), mean_mass = mean(body_mass_g, na.rm = TRUE))
    write_csv(result, path)
    result
}


Which of the functions above are pure? For each impure function, say which condition it breaks. Where you can, check your answers by experimenting.
Rewrite is_heavy so that it is pure.


Solution. 

to_kg is pure: its result depends only on mass_g, and it changes nothing.
is_heavy is impure, because its result depends on the global variable threshold as well as its argument. Changing threshold changes the answer, even though the argument is the same:


is_heavy(4500)

[1] TRUE

threshold <- 5000
is_heavy(4500)

[1] FALSE

threshold <- 4000


count_rows is impure, because it has a side effect: <<- changes the variable n_calls outside the function every time it is called. (Its result does depend only on its argument.)


count_rows(penguins)

[1] 344

count_rows(penguins)

[1] 344

n_calls

[1] 2



add_noise is impure, because it generates random numbers, so calling it twice with the same argument gives different results:


add_noise(1)

[1] 0.9790207

add_noise(1)

[1] 1.037817



drop_missing is pure, even though it seems to change its argument data. Assigning to data inside the function changes a local copy, and the tibble that was passed in is unchanged:


nrow(drop_missing(penguins))

[1] 342

nrow(penguins)

[1] 344



save_summary is impure, because writing a file is a side effect.

To make is_heavy pure, we pass the threshold in as an argument. Giving it a default value keeps calls such as is_heavy(4500) working:

is_heavy <- function(mass_g, threshold = 4000) mass_g > threshold
is_heavy(4500)

[1] TRUE

is_heavy(4500, threshold = 5000)

[1] FALSE




Extension: Rewrite save_summary as a pure function that computes the summary, and a separate step that writes it to a file. Why is this split easier to test?


Solution. 

summarise_mass <- function(data) {
    data |>
        summarise(n = n(), mean_mass = mean(body_mass_g, na.rm = TRUE))
}

mass_summary <- summarise_mass(penguins)
write_csv(mass_summary, "results/mass_summary.csv")
mass_summary

# A tibble: 1 × 2
      n mean_mass
  <int>     <dbl>
1   344     4202.


summarise_mass can now be tested by calling it on a small tibble whose answer we know, and checking what it returns, without creating any files that the test would have to read back and then tidy up. Writing the file becomes one line at the edge of the analysis, as the notes recommend: the side effects are kept few and in one place, and everything else is done by pure functions.

test_data <- tibble(body_mass_g = c(3000, 5000, NA))
stopifnot(summarise_mass(test_data)$n == 3)
stopifnot(summarise_mass(test_data)$mean_mass == 4000)





This task follows on from Task 2 of the lab, where you made fit_bill_model() check its input.

Write a function check_bill_model() that tests fit_bill_model(), in the style of check_distance() in the Week 9 notes. Include at least one test where you know the right answer, and one test that bad data are rejected with an error. (Hint: make up a tiny tibble whose points lie exactly on a line you choose.)


Solution. The points \((1, 3)\), \((2, 5)\) and \((3, 7)\) lie exactly on the line \(y = 2x + 1\), so the fitted slope must be 2 and the intercept 1. The second test uses a single complete penguin, which the lab showed is not enough to fit a line. Both test datasets are created inside the function, so that it doesn’t depend on any global variables:

check_bill_model <- function(fit_fn) {
    # points exactly on the line depth = 2 * length + 1
    on_line <- tibble(bill_length_mm = c(1, 2, 3), bill_depth_mm = c(3, 5, 7))
    result <- fit_fn(on_line)
    stopifnot(isTRUE(all.equal(result$slope, 2)))
    stopifnot(isTRUE(all.equal(result$intercept, 1)))
    # a single complete penguin is not enough to fit a line
    one_penguin <- tibble(bill_length_mm = c(40, NA), bill_depth_mm = c(18, 17))
    result <- try(fit_fn(one_penguin), silent = TRUE)
    stopifnot(inherits(result, "try-error"))
    "All tests passed."
}

check_bill_model(fit_bill_model)

[1] "All tests passed."


We compare with all.equal() rather than ==, because the fitted coefficients are not exactly 2 and 1, only very close:

on_line <- tibble(bill_length_mm = c(1, 2, 3), bill_depth_mm = c(3, 5, 7))
fit_bill_model(on_line)$intercept == 1

[1] FALSE


Writing the tests also exposes a surprise in the first version of fit_bill_model() from Task 1 of the lab, which extracted the slope with coef(model)["bill_length_mm"]. Single brackets keep the name of the element, so the slope is a named number, and all.equal() reports the difference in names, even though the values agree:

old_slope <- coef(lm(bill_depth_mm ~ bill_length_mm, data = on_line))["bill_length_mm"]
old_slope

bill_length_mm 
             2 

all.equal(old_slope, 2)

[1] "names for target but not for current"


Double brackets, [[, extract just the value, which is why the final version uses them.


Extension: Document fit_bill_model() with a roxygen comment. Then move it into a file R/models.R, and load it into your Quarto document with source().


Solution. The file R/models.R contains:
#' Fit a straight line of bill depth against bill length
#'
#' Fits a linear regression of bill depth on bill length, and returns
#' its slope and intercept.
#'
#' @param data A data frame with columns bill_length_mm and bill_depth_mm
#' @return A one-row tibble with columns slope and intercept
#' @examples
#' fit_bill_model(penguins)
fit_bill_model <- function(data) {
    n_complete <- sum(!is.na(data$bill_length_mm) & !is.na(data$bill_depth_mm))
    if (n_complete < 2) {
        stop("Need at least 2 penguins with both bill measurements, but found ", n_complete, ".")
    }
    model <- lm(bill_depth_mm ~ bill_length_mm, data = data)
    tibble(
        slope = coef(model)[["bill_length_mm"]],
        intercept = coef(model)[["(Intercept)"]]
    )
}
and the Quarto document loads it with

source("R/models.R")

The path is relative to the folder containing the Quarto document, so the project still works when it is moved to another computer.




This task follows on from Task 2 of the lab, and also uses the defensive checks from the end of it.

Write a function read_penguin_folder(path) that reads every CSV file in the folder path into a single tibble, with a column recording which file each row came from. Then try it with a misspelt folder name, such as "data/pengiuns". What happens, and why is it dangerous? Change your function so that it fails fast.


Solution. A first version just wraps the code from the lab in a function:

read_penguin_folder <- function(path) {
    list.files(path, pattern = "\\.csv$", full.names = TRUE) |>
        set_names() |>
        map(read_csv) |>
        list_rbind(names_to = "file")
}

read_penguin_folder("data/penguins") |> nrow()

[1] 344

read_penguin_folder("data/pengiuns")

data frame with 0 columns and 0 rows


With the misspelt name there is no error at all. list.files() doesn’t complain about a folder that doesn’t exist: it returns an empty vector of file names. Mapping over an empty vector gives an empty list, and list_rbind() turns that into a data frame with no rows and no columns. The problem only shows up later, when some other code looks for a column that isn’t there, far from its real cause:

read_penguin_folder("data/pengiuns") |> count(species)

Error in `count()`:
! Must group by variables found in `.data`.
✖ Column `species` is not found.


To fail fast, the function should check that it found some files before reading them:

read_penguin_folder <- function(path) {
    files <- list.files(path, pattern = "\\.csv$", full.names = TRUE)
    if (length(files) == 0) {
        stop("No CSV files found in '", path, "'. Is the folder name right?")
    }
    files |>
        set_names() |>
        map(read_csv) |>
        list_rbind(names_to = "file")
}


read_penguin_folder("data/pengiuns")

Error in read_penguin_folder("data/pengiuns"): No CSV files found in 'data/pengiuns'. Is the folder name right?






This task follows on from Task 2 of the lab, where you used possibly() to skip the files that could not be fitted.

possibly() skips failures silently. Instead, use tryCatch() to fit fit_bill_model() to each file in by_file, so that each file that can’t be fitted is skipped with a message saying which file it was and what went wrong. Combine the results for the other files into a single tibble.


Solution. The function needs to know the name of the file as well as its data, so that it can report it, so we map over both the tibbles and their names with map2. Inside the error function, conditionMessage(e) returns the error’s message: here, the clear message from our defensive fit_bill_model().

fit_or_report <- function(data, file) {
    tryCatch(
        fit_bill_model(data),
        error = function(e) {
            message("Skipping ", file, ": ", conditionMessage(e))
            NULL
        }
    )
}

file_fits <- map2(by_file, names(by_file), fit_or_report)

Skipping data/penguins/chinstrap_2008.csv: Need at least 2 penguins with both bill measurements, but found 0.

But each slope is estimated from only 24 to 52 penguins, so we should expect it to vary from year to year by chance, even if nothing has changed. title: Lab 7
text:
This lab accompanies the Week 7 notes, SQL for Data Science.

Read SQL queries, including joins, GROUP BY aggregations and HAVING, and explain what question they answer.

The database data/lego.sqlite contains information about LEGO sets released between 1950 and 2017, and the parts they contain. Its schema is shown in the figure below.

Before running it, write down in one sentence the question that it answers, and how many rows and columns you expect the result to have.

-- Query 1

Solution. Every line in the figure joins a foreign key to the primary key of another table:







Line
Relationship




themes.id – sets.theme_id
One theme has many sets; each set has one theme.


part_categories.id – parts.part_cat_id
One category has many parts; each part has one category.


sets.set_num – inventories.set_num
One set has many inventories; each inventory belongs to one set.


inventories.id – inventory_parts.inventory_id
One inventory has many rows in inventory_parts; each row belongs to one inventory.


parts.part_num – inventory_parts.part_num
One part has many rows in inventory_parts; each row is for one part.


colors.id – inventory_parts.color_id
One colour has many rows in inventory_parts; each row is in one colour.


inventories.id – inventory_sets.inventory_id
One inventory has many rows in inventory_sets; each row belongs to one inventory.


sets.set_num – inventory_sets.set_num
One set has many rows in inventory_sets; each row is for one set.



So every line is one-to-many, read from the primary key to the foreign key (or many-to-one, read the other way). This is no accident: a primary key is unique, so each row on the foreign key side can match only one row on the primary key side, whereas nothing stops many rows from sharing the same foreign key value.
The query counts the inventories of each set, and shows that set 421-2 has five, which are different versions of its parts list. Only 8 sets have more than one inventory (and 3 have none), so the relationship is almost one-to-one, but the database allows one-to-many. This matters when joining: a query that joins sets to inventories would count set 421-2 five times.
sets and parts are many-to-many: a set contains many different parts, and a part appears in many sets. A single line cannot represent this, because a column holds one value in each row. Instead, it goes through a linking table with one row for each combination: each set has an inventory (inventories), and inventory_parts has a row for each part, in each colour, in each inventory. This is why the natural key of inventory_parts combines several columns, as we will see next.
inventory_sets is another linking table, for sets that contain other sets. The third query joins each of its rows to the inventory, and then to the set that the inventory belongs to, giving the name of the containing set alongside each set it contains. For example, the inventory of the Star Wars Super Pack 2 in 1 contains the two sets 75048 and 75053. An inventory can contain many sets (up to 30) and a set can appear in many inventories (up to 12), so this relationship between inventories and sets is many-to-many too.

Finally, here is the CREATE TABLE statement that was used to create inventory_parts. (SQLite stores these statements in a special table called sqlite_master; we have tidied up its formatting.)
CREATE TABLE inventory_parts (
    inventory_id INTEGER,
    part_num TEXT,
    color_id INTEGER,
    quantity INTEGER,
    is_spare TEXT,
    FOREIGN KEY (color_id) REFERENCES colors(id),
    FOREIGN KEY (inventory_id) REFERENCES inventories(id),
    FOREIGN KEY (part_num) REFERENCES parts(part_num)
);

    collect()

sets |>
    select(num_parts) |>
    collect() |>
    summarise(p90 = quantile(num_parts, 0.9))

Solution. Every line in the figure joins a foreign key to the primary key of another table:







Line
Relationship




themes.id – sets.theme_id
One theme has many sets; each set has one theme.


part_categories.id – parts.part_cat_id
One category has many parts; each part has one category.


sets.set_num – inventories.set_num
One set has many inventories; each inventory belongs to one set.


inventories.id – inventory_parts.inventory_id
One inventory has many rows in inventory_parts; each row belongs to one inventory.


parts.part_num – inventory_parts.part_num
One part has many rows in inventory_parts; each row is for one part.


colors.id – inventory_parts.color_id
One colour has many rows in inventory_parts; each row is in one colour.


inventories.id – inventory_sets.inventory_id
One inventory has many rows in inventory_sets; each row belongs to one inventory.


sets.set_num – inventory_sets.set_num
One set has many rows in inventory_sets; each row is for one set.



So every line is one-to-many, read from the primary key to the foreign key (or many-to-one, read the other way). This is no accident: a primary key is unique, so each row on the foreign key side can match only one row on the primary key side, whereas nothing stops many rows from sharing the same foreign key value.
The query counts the inventories of each set, and shows that set 421-2 has five, which are different versions of its parts list. Only 8 sets have more than one inventory (and 3 have none), so the relationship is almost one-to-one, but the database allows one-to-many. This matters when joining: a query that joins sets to inventories would count set 421-2 five times.
sets and parts are many-to-many: a set contains many different parts, and a part appears in many sets. A single line cannot represent this, because a column holds one value in each row. Instead, it goes through a linking table with one row for each combination: each set has an inventory (inventories), and inventory_parts has a row for each part, in each colour, in each inventory. This is why the natural key of inventory_parts combines several columns, as we will see next.
inventory_sets is another linking table, for sets that contain other sets. The third query joins each of its rows to the inventory, and then to the set that the inventory belongs to, giving the name of the containing set alongside each set it contains. For example, the inventory of the Star Wars Super Pack 2 in 1 contains the two sets 75048 and 75053. An inventory can contain many sets (up to 30) and a set can appear in many inventories (up to 12), so this relationship between inventories and sets is many-to-many too.

Finally, here is the CREATE TABLE statement that was used to create inventory_parts. (SQLite stores these statements in a special table called sqlite_master; we have tidied up its formatting.)
CREATE TABLE inventory_parts (
    inventory_id INTEGER,
    part_num TEXT,
    color_id INTEGER,
    quantity INTEGER,
    is_spare TEXT,
    FOREIGN KEY (color_id) REFERENCES colors(id),
    FOREIGN KEY (inventory_id) REFERENCES inventories(id),
    FOREIGN KEY (part_num) REFERENCES parts(part_num)
);

inventory_parts has no primary key. What problems could this cause?
Suggest a primary key for inventory_parts. (Hint: no single column will do.)
The first query below tests one possible key. What does it count, and what does its result tell you? Use the second query to see an example, and improve your key if you need to.


SELECT COUNT(*) AS n_repeated
FROM (
    SELECT inventory_id, part_num, color_id
    FROM inventory_parts
    GROUP BY inventory_id, part_num, color_id
    HAVING COUNT(*) > 1
);


1 records


n_repeated




27324






SELECT *
FROM inventory_parts
WHERE inventory_id = 3 AND part_num = '33291' AND color_id = 191;


2 records


inventory_id
part_num
color_id
quantity
is_spare




3
33291
191
3
f


3
33291
191
1
t






Solution. Without a primary key, nothing stops the same row from being inserted twice, which would double-count parts. There is also no way to identify one particular row, for example to UPDATE or DELETE it, other than by listing all of its values.
Each row of inventory_parts says how many of one part, in one colour, are in one inventory, so a natural key combines inventory_id, part_num and color_id. The query groups the rows by these three columns, keeps the groups with more than one row, and counts those groups: 27,324 combinations appear more than once, so these three columns are not a valid key. The example shows why: inventory 3 contains three of part 33291 in colour 191, plus one more as a spare. Adding is_spare to the key fixes this: no combination of all four columns is repeated, so PRIMARY KEY (inventory_id, part_num, color_id, is_spare) would be a valid key.




In this task we query the same database using dplyr code, which dbplyr translates into SQL. The cell below creates a lazy table for each of the tables we need.

library(dbplyr)

themes <- tbl(con, "themes")
inventory_parts <- tbl(con, "inventory_parts")


Print sets. What does the ?? in the first line of the output mean, and why doesn’t dbplyr know the answer?

sets

sets is a lazy table: dbplyr has only fetched the first few rows, to show us, so it does not know how many rows the table has without running another query.


Write dplyr code that answers the same question as Query 3 from Task 1. Use show_query() to compare the SQL that dbplyr generates with Query 3.


Solution. 

year_most_sets <- sets |>
    group_by(year) |>
    summarise(n_sets = n()) |>
    arrange(desc(n_sets)) |>
    head(1)

show_query(year_most_sets)

<SQL>
SELECT `year`, COUNT(*) AS `n_sets`
FROM `sets`
GROUP BY `year`
ORDER BY `n_sets` DESC
LIMIT 1

collect(year_most_sets)

# A tibble: 1 × 2
   year n_sets
  <int>  <int>
1  2014    713


The generated SQL is the same as Query 3, apart from the backticks around names.


Write dplyr code to count the top-level themes, which have no parent. Use show_query() to see how dbplyr translates your code. Why would filter(parent_id == NA) not work?


Solution. 

top_level <- themes |>
    filter(is.na(parent_id)) |>
    summarise(n_top_level = n())

show_query(top_level)

<SQL>
SELECT COUNT(*) AS `n_top_level`
FROM (
  SELECT `themes`.*
  FROM `themes`
  WHERE ((`parent_id` IS NULL))
) AS `q01`

collect(top_level)

# A tibble: 1 × 1
  n_top_level
        <int>
1         111


dbplyr translates is.na(parent_id) into parent_id IS NULL. parent_id == NA would compare each value with “unknown”, which is never true, in R as well as in SQL; it is translated to parent_id = NULL, and keeps no rows:

themes |>
    filter(parent_id == NA) |>
    summarise(n_top_level = n()) |>
    collect()

# A tibble: 1 × 1
  n_top_level
        <int>
1           0



Next, we ask: are LEGO sets getting bigger?

Calculate the mean number of parts per set in each year, in the database, then collect the result and plot it.
473 sets have num_parts equal to 0. Find which themes most of these sets belong to. Should they be included in the mean? Redraw your plot without them.
What do you conclude? Look at the spike around 1960, and at the most recent year: how many sets is each point based on?


Solution. 

sets |>
    group_by(year) |>
    summarise(mean_parts = mean(num_parts, na.rm = TRUE), .groups = "drop") |>
    collect() |>
    ggplot(aes(x = year, y = mean_parts)) +
    geom_line() +
    labs(x = "Year", y = "Mean number of parts per set")








Everything before collect() runs in the database, so only one row per year is sent to R; ggplot then runs in R. (Without na.rm = TRUE, dbplyr warns that SQL always removes missing values when it aggregates.)

sets |>
    filter(num_parts == 0) |>
    count(theme_id) |>
    inner_join(themes, by = c("theme_id" = "id")) |>
    arrange(desc(n)) |>
    head(5) |>
    collect()

# A tibble: 5 × 4
  theme_id     n name         parent_id
     <int> <int> <chr>            <int>
1      501   181 Gear                NA
2      503   122 Key Chain          501
3      497    31 Books               NA
4      238    17 My Own Train       236
5      259    16 NXT                258


Most of the sets with no parts are Gear, key chains and books: they are not building sets, so they should be left out of an average set size.

sets |>
    filter(num_parts > 0) |>
    group_by(year) |>
    summarise(mean_parts = mean(num_parts, na.rm = TRUE), .groups = "drop") |>
    collect() |>
    ggplot(aes(x = year, y = mean_parts)) +
    geom_line() +
    labs(x = "Year", y = "Mean number of parts per set")








Sets have grown: the mean number of parts has risen from under 50 in the 1950s to over 200 in the 2010s. Not every point is equally reliable, though. Counting the sets behind each mean shows that the spike in 1960 is based on just two sets, one of which has 476 parts:

sets |>
    filter(num_parts > 0, year %in% c(1959, 1960, 1961, 2016, 2017)) |>
    group_by(year) |>
    summarise(
        n_sets = n(),
        mean_parts = mean(num_parts, na.rm = TRUE),
        .groups = "drop"
    ) |>
    collect()

# A tibble: 5 × 3
   year n_sets mean_parts
  <int>  <int>      <dbl>
1  1959      4       16.2
2  1960      2      263  
3  1961     16       75  
4  2016    587      257. 
5  2017    292      264. 


The data also stop part of the way through 2017, so the last point is based on about half as many sets as 2016, and these may not be a typical selection of the year’s sets.

Finally, we compare doing the work in the database with doing it in R. Both of the pipelines below count the total number of parts of each colour.

# Pipeline 1
inventory_parts |>
    group_by(color_id) |>
    summarise(total = sum(quantity, na.rm = TRUE), .groups = "drop") |>
    collect()

# Pipeline 2
inventory_parts |>
    collect() |>
    group_by(color_id) |>
    summarise(total = sum(quantity), .groups = "drop")


Which pipeline would you use, and why?
Try calculating the 90th percentile of num_parts with quantile() in the database. What happens? How can you fix it?


Solution. Both give the same result, but Pipeline 1 is better. It sums the quantities in the database and sends R one row per colour, whereas Pipeline 2 first copies all 580,069 rows of inventory_parts into R.
quantile() has no translation into SQLite’s SQL, so the query fails:

sets |>
    summarise(p90 = quantile(num_parts, 0.9)) |>
    collect()

Error in `quantile()`:
! `quantile()` is not available in this SQL variant.


To fix it, we collect just the column we need, and calculate the percentile in R:

sets |>
    select(num_parts) |>
    collect() |>
    summarise(p90 = quantile(num_parts, 0.9))

# A tibble: 1 × 1
    p90
  <dbl>
1   445



We have finished with the database, so we close the connection:

dbDisconnect(con)

title: Lab 10 Practice Questions
text:
These questions are for extra practice after Lab 10, using the same data. Task 1 follows on from Task 1 of the lab (chunks). Tasks 2 and 3 cover DuckDB, which the Week 10 notes describe but the lab does not use; they use the small file from the lab, apart from the last question of Task 2, which uses the larger file from Task 2 of the lab. Questions marked Extension are more challenging.
The cell below generates the data file if it isn’t already there (as in the lab), and recreates the full dataset and the map_reduce_chunked() function from Task 1 of the lab. Change n here if you want a different size of file; the last question of Task 2 does this.


Code
set.seed(2025)

n <- 100000L  # data rows
if (!dir.exists("data")) dir.create("data")
file_path <- paste0("data/large_data_", n, ".csv")  # path to data

generate_data <- function() {
    group <- sample(c("A","B","C","D"), n, replace = TRUE, prob = c(0.4, 0.3, 0.2, 0.1))
    dat <- data.frame(
        id = seq_len(n),
        timestamp = as.POSIXct("2020-01-01", tz = "UTC") + runif(n, 0, 365*24*3600),
        group = group,
        value = rnorm(n, mean = 100, sd = 20) + as.numeric(factor(group, levels = c("A","B","C","D"))) * 2 + rnorm(n, 0, 1)
    )

    dat$value <- round(dat$value, 2)

    readr::write_csv(dat, file_path)
    message("Wrote ", nrow(dat), " rows to ", file_path)
}
if (!file.exists(file_path)) generate_data()



library(tidyverse)

Warning: package 'dplyr' was built under R version 4.4.3

full_data <- read_csv(file_path)

map_reduce_chunked <- function(file, map_op, reduce_op, chunk_size = 1000) {
    results <- read_csv_chunked(
        file,
        callback = DataFrameCallback$new(map_op),
        chunk_size = chunk_size
    )
    results |> reduce(reduce_op)
}




Extension: What is the standard deviation of value for each group? Check your answer against sd() on the full data.


Solution. The standard deviation is different from a quantile, because it can be built from summaries that do combine exactly. The variance of \(n\) values is \[
s^2 = \frac{1}{n - 1}\left(\sum_i x_i^2 - \frac{\left(\sum_i x_i\right)^2}{n}\right),
\] so for each group, the map step only needs to return the sum of the values, the sum of their squares, and the count. All three can be added up across chunks, exactly as the sums and counts were for the mean.

map_group_sd <- function(chunk, pos) {
    list(
        chunk |>
            group_by(group) |>
            summarise(
                value_sum = sum(value),
                value_sq_sum = sum(value^2),
                value_count = n(),
                .groups = "drop"
            )
    )
}

reduce_group_sd <- function(cur, new) {
    bind_rows(cur, new) |>
        summarise(
            value_sum = sum(value_sum),
            value_sq_sum = sum(value_sq_sum),
            value_count = sum(value_count),
            .by = group
        )
}

sd_result <- map_reduce_chunked(file_path, map_group_sd, reduce_group_sd) |>
    mutate(
        variance = (value_sq_sum - value_sum^2 / value_count) / (value_count - 1),
        sd = sqrt(variance)
    ) |>
    select(group, sd) |>
    arrange(group)
sd_result

# A tibble: 4 × 2
  group    sd
  <chr> <dbl>
1 A      20.1
2 B      19.9
3 C      20.1
4 D      19.9

# validate with the full dataset
full_data |> group_by(group) |> summarise(sd = sd(value))

# A tibble: 4 × 2
  group    sd
  <chr> <dbl>
1 A      20.1
2 B      19.9
3 C      20.1
4 D      19.9


The two agree. (This formula can lose accuracy when the values are very large compared with their spread, because it subtracts two big numbers that are almost equal; it is fine for data like these.)




The following code replicates the sum in Task 1 of the lab using duckplyr, a layer over duckdb that allows use of dplyr syntax.

# Load required libraries
library(duckplyr)

The duckplyr package is configured to fall back to dplyr when it encounters an
incompatibility. Fallback events can be collected and uploaded for analysis to
guide future development. By default, data will be collected but no data will
be uploaded.
ℹ Automatic fallback uploading is not controlled and therefore disabled, see
  `?duckplyr::fallback()`.
✔ Number of reports ready for upload: 103.
→ Review with `duckplyr::fallback_review()`, upload with
  `duckplyr::fallback_upload()`.
ℹ Configure automatic uploading with `duckplyr::fallback_config()`.


✔ Overwriting dplyr methods with duckplyr methods.
ℹ Turn off with `duckplyr::methods_restore()`.

# Register the CSV file as a table
data <- read_csv_duckdb(file_path, prudence="stingy")

# Create a virtual table for the CSV file
data |> summarize(value_sum=sum(value))

# A duckplyr data frame: 1 variable
  value_sum
      <dbl>
1 10391834.



Extension: What is the sum of value for group A?
Extension: Try to compute the sums of value for each group. (Hint: use #| error: true at the start of your code cell to see any errors this produces.)
Extension: Use the error message to find a way to compute the sums of value for each group that still runs inside DuckDB.
Extension: Now experiment with the prudence option above. Which settings let group_by() work, and what is the downside? How does it compare to using read_csv_chunked?
Extension: Set n to 3000000L in the set-up code above and run it again, then repeat the prudence experiment on the larger file. What changes?


Solution. This query is fine because it can be done in a single sweep.

data |> filter(group == "A") |> summarise(value_sum = sum(value))

# A duckplyr data frame: 1 variable
  value_sum
      <dbl>
1  4064210.


However, duckplyr refuses to run the group_by() version, because it would have to load the whole dataset into R to do so:

data |> group_by(group) |> summarise(value_sum = sum(value))

Error in `group_by()`:
! This operation cannot be carried out by DuckDB, and the input is a
  stingy duckplyr frame.
• Try `summarise(.by = ...)` or `mutate(.by = ...)` instead of `group_by()` and
  `ungroup()`.
ℹ Use `compute(prudence = "lavish")` to materialize to temporary storage and
  continue with duckplyr.
ℹ See `vignette("prudence")` for other options.


The error message suggests the fix: summarise() has a .by argument, which gives the same result as group_by() followed by summarise(), but which DuckDB can run.

data |> summarise(value_sum = sum(value), .by = group)

# A duckplyr data frame: 2 variables
  group value_sum
  <chr>     <dbl>
1 B      3120407.
2 A      4064210.
3 D      1079781.
4 C      2127435.


The data stay in DuckDB, which reads through the file once, and only the four-row result comes back to R.
The other route is to change prudence, which controls how willing duckplyr is to fall back on ordinary dplyr, and so to load the data into R’s memory. With "lavish" the grouped query runs, because duckplyr simply loads the whole dataset into memory, and then uses dplyr:

data_lavish <- read_csv_duckdb(file_path, prudence = "lavish")
data_lavish |> group_by(group) |> summarise(value_sum = sum(value))

# A tibble: 4 × 2
  group value_sum
  <chr>     <dbl>
1 A      4064210.
2 B      3120407.
3 C      2127435.
4 D      1079781.


The downside is that this is exactly the problem we were trying to avoid: for a file too big for memory, the query would fail or crash R. The default, "thrifty", is a middle ground: it only loads data into memory if they are small (fewer than a million cells). It happens to work here, because our file has only 100,000 rows of four columns, but it would give the same error as "stingy" on a genuinely large file. So the setting that “works” is only safe when the data are small enough that we didn’t need DuckDB in the first place.
Compared to read_csv_chunked, .by gives the same answer with no work on our part: we don’t have to write the map and reduce steps, or work out which summaries (sums and counts) can be combined. The cost is that it only works for the operations that DuckDB supports, whereas the chunked approach lets us run any R code on each chunk.
For the prudence experiment, the default prudence = "thrifty" now gives the same error as "stingy" for the grouped query, because the table is too big for duckplyr to be willing to load into memory. The query summarise(value_sum = sum(value), .by = group) still works. Only prudence = "lavish" would let group_by() through, by loading the whole file into memory. So the choice of prudence that “worked” on the small file was working only because the data were small.





The Week 10 notes show a second way to query a CSV file with DuckDB, using DBI and dbplyr as in Week 9. Use it to compute the sums of value for each group, and look at the SQL that is written. Why does group_by() work here when it didn’t with duckplyr?


Solution. We connect to a temporary DuckDB database, and duckdb::tbl_file() gives a lazy table that reads directly from the CSV file, without loading it into R.

library(DBI)
library(dbplyr)

con <- dbConnect(duckdb::duckdb())
data_db <- duckdb::tbl_file(con, file_path)

query <- data_db |>
    group_by(group) |>
    summarise(value_sum = sum(value, na.rm = TRUE), .groups = "drop")

show_query(query)

<SQL>
SELECT "group", SUM("value") AS value_sum
FROM (FROM 'data/large_data_100000.csv') q01
GROUP BY "group"


The FROM clause names the CSV file itself, rather than a table in the database. Running the query gives the same sums as before:

query |> collect()

# A tibble: 4 × 2
  group value_sum
  <chr>     <dbl>
1 A      4064210.
2 C      2127435.
3 D      1079781.
4 B      3120407.



dbDisconnect(con)

The grouped query works because dbplyr never runs group_by() in R. It translates the whole pipeline into one SQL query, with a GROUP BY clause, and sends it to DuckDB, which reads through the file and returns only the four-row result. duckplyr instead tries to run each step itself, and when it meets a step it can’t run inside DuckDB (as with group_by()), it has to decide whether to load the data into R’s memory, which is what prudence controls. With dbplyr, there is no such decision to make: we have chosen to work in the database, so the query has to be one that SQL can express.
