Getting data to load without an error is only the first step: R will happily load data in a way that is wrong. You should always check that what you have loaded makes sense. In this task we will look more closely at the three files from Task 1.
The file data3 contains information about books in a bookshop.

Look at the type of each column. Is the ISBN column stored sensibly? (Hint: an ISBN is an identifier; would it make sense to add two ISBNs together? What would happen to an ISBN that starts with a 0?)
Reload the file so that ISBN is stored as text. (Hint: look up the col_types argument of read_delim, and the cols and col_character functions.)
readr also has a function called read_csv2, which reads files that use ; as a delimiter. Try loading data3 with read_csv2 instead. Compare the PriceUSD and AvgRating columns to the raw file. What has gone wrong?


Solution. 

books <- read_delim(
    "data/part1/data3",
    delim = ";",
    col_types = cols(ISBN = col_character()),
    show_col_types = FALSE
)
books |> select(Title, ISBN)

# A tibble: 12 × 2
   Title                       ISBN         
   <chr>                       <chr>        
 1 The Copper Orchard          9780143127741
 2 Patterns of Quiet           9780307269997
 3 Practical Urban Foraging    9781982134520
 4 Circuit Stories             9780525555360
 5 Handmade Typography         9781593279509
 6 Tides of Reason             9780307743657
 7 Introduction to Wild Baking 9781449340377
 8 Maps for Modern Gardens     9780062871253
 9 The Last Radio              9780143128571
10 Data Without Tears          9780307474278
11 A Walk Through Rust         9780735211303
12 Quiet Machines              9781590599992


ISBN was originally read as a number (<dbl>), because it consists only of digits. However it is an identifier, not a quantity: arithmetic on it is meaningless, and any leading zeros would be lost. It should be stored as text.

read_csv2("data/part1/data3", show_col_types = FALSE) |>
    select(Title, PriceUSD, AvgRating) |>
    head()

ℹ Using "','" as decimal and "'.'" as grouping mark. Use `read_delim()` for more control.


# A tibble: 6 × 3
  Title                    PriceUSD AvgRating
  <chr>                       <dbl>     <dbl>
1 The Copper Orchard           1499        42
2 Patterns of Quiet            1250        46
3 Practical Urban Foraging     1800        40
4 Circuit Stories              1625        44
5 Handmade Typography          2700        47
6 Tides of Reason              1099        39


read_csv2 is designed for the convention used in much of Europe, where ; is the delimiter and , is the decimal mark (e.g. 14,99). It therefore treats the . in 14.99 as a thousands separator, so the price 14.99 becomes 1499 and the rating 4.2 becomes 42. Notice that R did not give an error; the only warning was an info message that is easy to ignore. This is why you should always check your loaded data against the raw file!

The file data1.csv contains student scores from two tests, with their average.

How are missing scores recorded in the raw file, and what do they become when loaded into R? What else in the file was loaded as missing?
Compute the mean of score1. Why do you get NA, and how can you fix this? (Hint: look at how na.rm was used in the notes.)
Look at the row for Henry Zhao. Are his scores really 0? What happens to the mean of score1 and of average if he is excluded?


Solution. 

students <- read_csv("data/part1/data1.csv", show_col_types = FALSE)
students

# A tibble: 10 × 9
      id name           age signup_date score1 score2 average passed notes      
   <dbl> <chr>        <dbl> <date>       <dbl>  <dbl>   <dbl> <lgl>  <chr>      
 1     1 Alice Smith     22 2025-02-01    88.5   91      89.8 TRUE   Consistent…
 2     2 Bob Jones       24 2024-09-15    76     82.5    79.2 TRUE   Improved a…
 3     3 Carol Lee       21 2025-01-20    59     64      61.5 FALSE  Needs tuto…
 4     4 David Kim       23 2024-12-05    93.5   90      91.8 TRUE   Excellent  
 5     5 Eva Martín      22 2025-03-03    85     NA      85   TRUE   Missing se…
 6     6 Frank O'Neil    25 2024-10-30    NA     70      70   FALSE  Missing fi…
 7     7 Grace Li        20 2025-04-10    72     68      70   TRUE   Borderline…
 8     8 Henry Zhao      24 2025-02-28     0      0       0   FALSE  Absent     
 9     9 Ivy Chen        22 2024-11-11    88     92      90   TRUE   <NA>       
10    10 Jack Müller     23 2025-01-05    79.5   74      76.8 TRUE   Participat…


Missing scores are recorded as empty fields (e.g. 85.0,,85.00), which read_csv converts to NA. The empty notes for Ivy Chen ("") has also been read as NA.

students |>
    summarise(mean_score1 = mean(score1), mean_score1_narm = mean(score1, na.rm = TRUE))

# A tibble: 1 × 2
  mean_score1 mean_score1_narm
        <dbl>            <dbl>
1          NA             71.3


Any calculation involving an NA gives NA, since R can’t know what the missing value is. Setting na.rm = TRUE removes the missing values before computing the mean.

students |>
    filter(name != "Henry Zhao") |>
    summarise(mean_score1 = mean(score1, na.rm = TRUE), mean_average = mean(average))

# A tibble: 1 × 2
  mean_score1 mean_average
        <dbl>        <dbl>
1        80.2         79.3


Henry’s notes say he was “Absent”, so his scores of 0 really mean “did not take the test”, and should arguably be missing (NA) rather than 0. Including him lowers the mean of score1 from about 80 to about 71. Whether that is right depends on the question: for “how well did students who sat the test do?” he should be excluded, but for “what marks were awarded?” a 0 might be correct. This kind of problem can’t be detected by R; you have to look at the data.

The file data2.txt contains readings from air quality monitoring stations.

Create a tibble containing only station_id and the particulate matter readings (the columns measured in µg/m³). Use a tidyselect helper rather than typing out the column names.


Solution. 

air_quality <- read_tsv("data/part1/data2.txt", show_col_types = FALSE)

air_quality |>
    select(station_id, ends_with("_ug_m3"))

The two particulate columns both end in _ug_m3, so ends_with selects them without listing them by hand.


How many readings are there in the file, and from how many different neighbourhoods? (Hint: look at the “Other Summarise Functions” tip in the notes.)


Solution. 

air_quality |>
    summarise(n_readings = n(), n_neighbourhoods = n_distinct(neighborhood))

# A tibble: 1 × 2
  n_readings n_neighbourhoods
       <int>            <int>
1         18               10


n() counts the rows, while n_distinct() counts the number of unique values in a column.


Which readings have a status other than OK? What do you notice about their pollution readings and sensor_uptime_pct?
Compute the mean pm2_5_ug_m3 over all readings, and over only the readings with status OK. Which would you report, and why?


Solution. 

air_quality |>
    filter(status != "OK") |>
    select(station_id, neighborhood, pm2_5_ug_m3, pm10_ug_m3, sensor_uptime_pct, status)

# A tibble: 3 × 6
  station_id neighborhood pm2_5_ug_m3 pm10_ug_m3 sensor_uptime_pct status
  <chr>      <chr>              <dbl>      <dbl>             <dbl> <chr> 
1 AQ-006     Harbor                55         82                95 MAINT 
2 AQ-012     Riverside             NA         NA                60 ERROR 
3 AQ-015     Harbor                60         90                95 MAINT 


Station AQ-012 has status ERROR, a low uptime, and no pollution readings at all (NA). The two MAINT readings, both in Harbor, do have values, but a sensor under maintenance may not be reliable.

air_quality |>
    summarise(mean_pm2_5 = mean(pm2_5_ug_m3, na.rm = TRUE))

# A tibble: 1 × 1
  mean_pm2_5
       <dbl>
1         43

air_quality |>
    filter(status == "OK") |>
    summarise(mean_pm2_5 = mean(pm2_5_ug_m3))

# A tibble: 1 × 1
  mean_pm2_5
       <dbl>
1       41.1


Removing the ERROR reading happens automatically with na.rm = TRUE, but the MAINT readings are only removed if we filter on status. Reporting the mean over OK readings only is the safer choice, but whatever you choose, you should say which readings were excluded and why.




The diamonds dataset is included as a part of ggplot2. If you have loaded tidyverse it should be already in your environment.

library(tidyverse)
diamonds

# A tibble: 53,940 × 10
   carat cut       color clarity depth table price     x     y     z
   <dbl> <ord>     <ord> <ord>   <dbl> <dbl> <int> <dbl> <dbl> <dbl>

It contains information about 53940 diamonds. Each row is a diamond, and each column contains information about that diamond such as:

price: The price of the diamond in US dollars.
carat: The weight of the diamond (1 carat = 0.2g).
cut: Quality of the cut.
color: The color of the diamond.
clarity: A measure of how clear the diamond is.
depth: Total depth percentage; \(= \frac{z}{\frac{1}{2}(x + y)} \times 100\).
table: Width of the top of the diamond relative to the widest point.
x: Length of the diamond in mm.
y: Width of the diamond in mm.
z: Depth of the diamond in mm.

For the next few tasks you should use dplyr functions, using pipe syntax. Try to format your code nicely so it is readable.

Add a new column to the tibble called volume that contains the volume of the diamond (\(x \times y \times z\)).


Solution. 

diamonds <- diamonds |> mutate(volume = x * y * z)



Create a tibble containing only the numeric columns of diamonds. (Hint: look at the tidyselect callout in the notes.)


Solution. 

diamonds |> select(where(is.numeric))

# A tibble: 53,940 × 8
   carat depth table price     x     y     z volume
   <dbl> <dbl> <dbl> <int> <dbl> <dbl> <dbl>  <dbl>
 1  0.23  61.5    55   326  3.95  3.98  2.43   38.2
 2  0.21  59.8    61   326  3.89  3.84  2.31   34.5
 3  0.23  56.9    65   327  4.05  4.07  2.31   38.1
 4  0.29  62.4    58   334  4.2   4.23  2.63   46.7
 5  0.31  63.3    58   335  4.34  4.35  2.75   51.9
 6  0.24  62.8    57   336  3.94  3.96  2.48   38.7

The file data/part3/assessment.csv contains a messy student scores table. It records the student’s scores out of 100 across 8 possible assessments. However, not all students take all assessments, and assessments the student has not taken are recorded as NA.

The table is not tidy. Each observation is one student’s score on one assessment, and the variables are the student, the semester, the assessment and the score.

Each variable is a column: the semester and the assessment are variables, but their values (e.g. Semester1, A1) are stored in the column names rather than in columns of their own.
Each observation is a row: each row contains up to 8 observations (one per assessment) rather than one.

Each cell does contain a single value, so the third rule is satisfied, for now!


Tidy the table: pivot into long format with one row per student and assessment, and drop missing scores.
Compute each student’s overall average, and the number of assessments they took. (Hint: look at the “Other Summarise Functions” tip in the notes.)

student_data_long <- student_data |>
    pivot_longer(
        cols = -student_id,
        names_to = "assessment",
        values_to = "score"

    drop_na(score)

    group_by(student_id) |>
    summarise(mean_score = mean(score), n_assessments = n(), .groups = "drop") |>

Both approaches give the same result here. However, -student_id means “every column except student_id”, so a new student_name column would be pivoted too, mixing names in with the scores (in fact pivot_longer would give an error, since it can’t combine text and numbers in one column). starts_with("Semester") only picks out the assessment columns, so it would keep working. Choosing columns by what they are, rather than by what they are not, is usually more robust.

One of the key principles of tidy data is that each cell should contain only one value. Notice that in the new dataset, the column assessment contains two values: the Semester and the Assessment ID, separated by an _.

Use separate_wider_delim to split assessment into two columns, one with the assessment ID and one with the Semester.
Create a wide table with one row per student, and two new columns containing the average score in Semester 1 and Semester 2.

title: Lab 5 Practice Questions
text:
These questions are for extra practice after Lab 5, using the same data. Each section follows on from the matching task in lab_05.qmd, so do that task first. Questions marked Extension are more challenging.
The cell below loads the data we used in the lab.

library(tidyverse)

Warning: package 'dplyr' was built under R version 4.4.3

library(janitor)
simpsons_characters <- read_csv("data/simpsons/simpsons_characters.csv")
simpsons_episodes <- read_csv("data/simpsons/simpsons_episodes.csv")
simpsons_locations <- read_csv("data/simpsons/simpsons_locations.csv")
simpsons_script_lines <- read_csv("data/simpsons/simpsons_script_lines.csv")
stock_data <- read_csv("data/all_stocks_5yr.csv") |>
    clean_names()



These questions follow on from Tasks 1 and 1b of the lab. (Make sure your outputs print character names, not just IDs).

Which characters have lines in the most episodes?
Extension: Which characters appear together most frequently in episodes?


Solution. Which characters have lines in the most episodes?
We count the episodes for each character_id first, and only then join to simpsons_characters to get the names. This way the join is done on a small summary table (one row per character) rather than on all 158,255 script lines.

simpsons_script_lines |>
    group_by(character_id) |>
    summarise(num_episodes = n_distinct(episode_id), .groups = "drop") |>
    arrange(desc(num_episodes)) |>
    inner_join(simpsons_characters, by = c("character_id" = "id")) |>
    select(character_name, num_episodes) |>
    head(10)

# A tibble: 10 × 2
   character_name      num_episodes
   <chr>                      <int>
 1 Homer Simpson                564
 2 Marge Simpson                563
 3 Bart Simpson                 562
 4 Lisa Simpson                 562
 5 Moe Szyslak                  376
 6 Milhouse Van Houten          325
 7 Lenny Leonard                319
 8 Chief Wiggum                 318
 9 Seymour Skinner              297
10 Carl Carlson                 282


Notice that grouping by character_id also creates a group for NA, the scene directions with no character (see Task 1 of the lab). This group appears in 564 episodes, tying with Homer for first place! The inner_join quietly removes it, because NA has no match in simpsons_characters; with a left_join it would appear near the top of the table with no name. It would be clearer still to remove it on purpose, with filter(!is.na(character_id)) before grouping.
Which characters appear together most frequently in episodes?
First we make a table with one row for each character in each episode, dropping the scene directions (which have no character):

episode_characters <- simpsons_script_lines |>
    filter(!is.na(character_id)) |>
    select(episode_id, character_id) |>
    distinct()

To find pairs of characters in the same episode, we join this table to itself on episode_id. Each episode has many characters on both sides of the join, so this is a many-to-many join: every character in an episode is matched with every other character in that episode. As the notes say, dplyr warns about many-to-many joins because they are often a mistake, but here it is exactly what we want, so we say so with relationship = "many-to-many", which also silences the warning.

episode_characters |>
    inner_join(episode_characters, by = "episode_id", relationship = "many-to-many") |>
    # both tables have a character_id column, so they get .x and .y suffixes.
    # Keeping only character_id.x < character_id.y removes each character paired
    # with themselves, and counts each pair once rather than twice (as A-B and B-A).
    filter(character_id.x < character_id.y) |>
    group_by(character_id.x, character_id.y) |>
    summarise(episodes_together = n(), .groups = "drop") |>

Which characters have lines in the most episodes?
Extension: Which characters appear together most frequently in episodes?


Solution. Which characters have lines in the most episodes?
We count the episodes for each character_id first, and only then join to simpsons_characters to get the names. This way the join is done on a small summary table (one row per character) rather than on all 158,255 script lines.

simpsons_script_lines |>
    group_by(character_id) |>
    summarise(num_episodes = n_distinct(episode_id), .groups = "drop") |>
    arrange(desc(num_episodes)) |>
    inner_join(simpsons_characters, by = c("character_id" = "id")) |>
    select(character_name, num_episodes) |>
    head(10)

# A tibble: 10 × 2
   character_name      num_episodes
   <chr>                      <int>
 1 Homer Simpson                564
 2 Marge Simpson                563
 3 Bart Simpson                 562
 4 Lisa Simpson                 562
 5 Moe Szyslak                  376
 6 Milhouse Van Houten          325
 7 Lenny Leonard                319
 8 Chief Wiggum                 318
 9 Seymour Skinner              297
10 Carl Carlson                 282


Notice that grouping by character_id also creates a group for NA, the scene directions with no character (see Task 1 of the lab). This group appears in 564 episodes, tying with Homer for first place! The inner_join quietly removes it, because NA has no match in simpsons_characters; with a left_join it would appear near the top of the table with no name. It would be clearer still to remove it on purpose, with filter(!is.na(character_id)) before grouping.
Which characters appear together most frequently in episodes?
First we make a table with one row for each character in each episode, dropping the scene directions (which have no character):

episode_characters <- simpsons_script_lines |>
    filter(!is.na(character_id)) |>
    select(episode_id, character_id) |>
    distinct()

To find pairs of characters in the same episode, we join this table to itself on episode_id. Each episode has many characters on both sides of the join, so this is a many-to-many join: every character in an episode is matched with every other character in that episode. As the notes say, dplyr warns about many-to-many joins because they are often a mistake, but here it is exactly what we want, so we say so with relationship = "many-to-many", which also silences the warning.

episode_characters |>
    inner_join(episode_characters, by = "episode_id", relationship = "many-to-many") |>
    # both tables have a character_id column, so they get .x and .y suffixes.
    # Keeping only character_id.x < character_id.y removes each character paired
    # with themselves, and counts each pair once rather than twice (as A-B and B-A).
    filter(character_id.x < character_id.y) |>
    group_by(character_id.x, character_id.y) |>
    summarise(episodes_together = n(), .groups = "drop") |>
    # join back to characters twice, to get both names (again with .x and .y suffixes)
    left_join(simpsons_characters, by = c("character_id.x" = "id")) |>
    left_join(simpsons_characters, by = c("character_id.y" = "id")) |>
    select(character_name.x, character_name.y, episodes_together) |>
    arrange(desc(episodes_together)) |>
    head(20)

title: Lab 10
text:
This lab accompanies the Week 10 notes, Working with Big Data.

Check how big a dataset really is, and read only the part of it you need.
Process a large file in chunks with read_csv_chunked(), using a “map” step and a “reduce” step.
Understand which summaries can be combined exactly across chunks, and which cannot.
See how these methods behave on a larger file, and when chunking pays off.

When you have finished the lab, there are more questions on the same data in lab_10_practice.qmd, including standard deviations from chunks, and using DuckDB to do the work in a database.


The code below generates a large amount of dummy data for you to work with. It has two important parameters:

n: the number of rows
file_path: the path of the file written to

The data file contains four columns:

An id
A timestamp
A group (A, B, C or D)
A (numeric) value



Code
set.seed(2025)

n <- 100000L  # data rows
if (!dir.exists("data")) dir.create("data")
file_path <- paste0("data/large_data_", n, ".csv")  # path to data

generate_data <- function() {
    group <- sample(c("A","B","C","D"), n, replace = TRUE, prob = c(0.4, 0.3, 0.2, 0.1))
    dat <- data.frame(
        id = seq_len(n),
        timestamp = as.POSIXct("2020-01-01", tz = "UTC") + runif(n, 0, 365*24*3600),
        group = group,
        value = rnorm(n, mean = 100, sd = 20) + as.numeric(factor(group, levels = c("A","B","C","D"))) * 2 + rnorm(n, 0, 1)
    )

    dat$value <- round(dat$value, 2)

    readr::write_csv(dat, file_path)
    message("Wrote ", nrow(dat), " rows to ", file_path)
}
if (!file.exists(file_path)) generate_data()


Wrote 100000 rows to data/large_data_100000.csv








NoteThis isn’t really “big” data



The file has 100,000 rows and is only about 3.5MB. It easily fits in memory, and read_csv() reads it in a fraction of a second. Genuinely big data would be tedious to work with in a short lab, because most of the time would be spent waiting. This data is big enough to give you an idea of how the tools work, but not big enough to be a problem. Task 2 uses a larger file to show what changes.


Before working with the data in chunks, let’s check how big it actually is (see “Is my data actually big?” in the Week 10 notes).

How large is the data file on disk, in MB? (Hint: file.size() gives the size in bytes.)
Read the file into a tibble with read_csv(). How much memory does it use? How does this compare with the size of the file?
Now read only the group and value columns. How does the memory used change?
Read only the first 1000 rows. When might this be useful, and what is the risk?
Do you need the tools in the rest of this lab for this data?


Solution. The file is about 3.5MB.

library(tidyverse)

Warning: package 'dplyr' was built under R version 4.4.3

file.size(file_path) / 1e6

[1] 3.534499


Once it is loaded into a tibble, the data take up about the same amount of memory as the file does on disk. The size on disk is a rough guide to the memory needed.

full_data <- read_csv(file_path)
format(object.size(full_data), units = "MB")

[1] "3.1 Mb"


Reading only the two columns we need uses roughly half the memory, because we no longer store id and timestamp. This can make a big difference if a file has many columns but the analysis uses only a few.

two_columns <- read_csv(file_path, col_select = c(group, value))
format(object.size(two_columns), units = "MB")

[1] "1.5 Mb"


n_max reads only the first rows, which is useful for writing and testing code quickly before running it on the whole file. The risk is that the first rows may not be representative of the rest: for example, if the file were sorted by group, we would see only group A. Here the rows are in a random order, so the first 1000 rows happen to be representative, with the groups in roughly the proportions of the whole file.

read_csv(file_path, n_max = 1000) |> count(group)

# A tibble: 4 × 2
  group     n
  <chr> <int>
1 A       384
2 B       305
3 C       204
4 D       107


For this data, no. The whole file fits in memory many times over and loads in a fraction of a second, so read_csv() would be the right tool. We use chunks here to learn how they work; they pay off only when the data are too big to load.

The following code applies the map / reduce paradigm to sum a column in a “large” data file using readr::read_csv_chunked.

# Load required libraries
library(tidyverse)

# Define a callback function to process each chunk
process_chunk <- function(chunk, pos) {
  chunk |>
    summarize(chunk_sum = sum(value, na.rm = TRUE)) |>
    pull()
}

# Process data in chunks, with timing
start.time <- Sys.time()
# This performs the "map" step.
chunk_results <- read_csv_chunked(
  file_path,
  callback = DataFrameCallback$new(process_chunk),
  chunk_size = 1000
)


── Column specification ────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
cols(
  id = col_double(),
  timestamp = col_datetime(format = ""),
  group = col_character(),
  value = col_double()
)

end.time <- Sys.time()
print(paste0("It took ", end.time - start.time, " seconds"))

[1] "It took 0.0807700157165527 seconds"

final_result <- chunk_results |>
  reduce(`+`)

print(final_result)

[1] 10391834


Modify the code above to answer the following questions:

Vary the chunk_size between 10, 100, 1000, 10000, 100000. Check the timings for each chunk_size. What do you notice?
What is the sum of value for group A?
What are the sums of value for each group? (Hint: try to write the map first, and check what it returns. Then think about the best way to perform the Reduce. You can do it with the reduce function, but you don’t need to!)
What is the mean of value for each group? (Hint: is the mean of the chunk means the same as the overall mean?)
Could you use this approach to compute the quantiles of value? Explain why, or why not?


Solution. Timings depend on your computer, but you should see the same pattern. On one run (median of five), the whole file took:



chunk_size
10
100
1000
10000
100000




Time (seconds)
0.45
0.04
0.03
0.04
0.15



Very small chunks are slow: with chunk_size = 10 the callback is called 10,000 times, and each call has a fixed cost (setting up the chunk, running the function, storing the result) that has nothing to do with how much data is in the chunk. Making the chunks bigger spreads this cost over more rows, which is why the time drops quickly between 10 and 1000.
But bigger is not always faster: the fastest value here is in the middle, and the single chunk of 100,000 rows (the whole file) was slower than 1000-row chunks. Since the point of chunking is to keep only one chunk in memory at a time, there is no benefit in making chunks larger than needed. A good chunk_size is large enough to make the per-chunk overhead small, and small enough that a chunk fits comfortably in memory. (With only 100,000 rows all of these are fast; the differences matter much more on a file with hundreds of millions of rows.)
For the questions, first we load the full dataset (for validation purposes) and define a generic function for the map / reduce.

full_data <- read_csv(file_path)

map_reduce_chunked <- function(file, map_op, reduce_op, chunk_size = 1000) {
    results <- read_csv_chunked(
        file,
        callback = DataFrameCallback$new(map_op),
        chunk_size = chunk_size
    )
    results |> reduce(reduce_op)
}

What is the sum of value for group A?
This is simple because we just need to filter.

map_a <- function(chunk, pos) {
    chunk |> filter(group == "A") |> summarise(value_sum = sum(value)) |> pull()
}

map_reduce_chunked(file_path, map_a, `+`)

[1] 4064210


What are the sums of value for each group?
This is more complex because the map step must now return a tibble, with one row per group, rather than a single number. By default, read_csv_chunked stacks the tibbles from all the chunks on top of each other. From this output it’s straightforward to use tidyverse functions to do the “reduce”: group again, and add up the partial sums.

map_group <- function(chunk, pos) {
    chunk |>
        group_by(group) |>
        summarise(value_sum = sum(value), .groups = "drop")
}

results <- read_csv_chunked(
    file_path,
    callback = DataFrameCallback$new(map_group),
    chunk_size = 1000
)
results |>
    group_by(group) |>
    summarise(value_sum = sum(value_sum), .groups = "drop")

# A tibble: 4 × 2
  group value_sum
  <chr>     <dbl>
1 A      4064210 
2 B      3120407.
3 C      2127435.
4 D      1079781.


Alternatively, we can write the reduce step ourselves, and pass it to reduce(). Now the callback has to return each chunk’s tibble inside a list(). Otherwise read_csv_chunked would stack the tibbles into one before reduce() sees it, and reduce() would try to combine the columns of that single tibble instead of the chunks. The reduce step takes the running total so far (cur) and the next chunk’s summary (new), stacks them and adds up again, so the result is always one row per group.

map_group_list <- function(chunk, pos) {
    list(
        chunk |>
            group_by(group) |>
            summarise(value_sum = sum(value), .groups = "drop")
    )
}

reduce_group <- function(cur, new) {
    bind_rows(cur, new) |>
        summarise(value_sum = sum(value_sum), .by = group)
}

map_reduce_chunked(file_path, map_group_list, reduce_group)

# A tibble: 4 × 2
  group value_sum
  <chr>     <dbl>
1 A      4064210 
2 B      3120407.
3 C      2127435.
4 D      1079781.


Stacking the two tibbles and summing again is safer than joining them by group. With an inner_join, any group missing from one chunk would be dropped altogether, which is quite possible with small chunks: with chunk_size = 10 an inner_join version returns no rows at all.
From here it is a simple extension to get the mean, by just adding the count of values to the summary. We must not return the mean of each chunk: means of chunks of different sizes can’t simply be averaged, but sums and counts can be added up exactly.

map_group_mean <- function(chunk, pos) {
    list(
        chunk |>
            group_by(group) |>
            summarise(value_sum = sum(value), value_count = n(), .groups = "drop")
    )
}

    bind_rows(cur, new) |>
        summarise(
            value_sum = sum(value_sum),
            value_count = sum(value_count),
            .by = group
        )
}

    mutate(mean = value_sum / value_count) |>
    select(group, mean)
mean_result

# A tibble: 4 × 2
  group  mean
  <chr> <dbl>
1 A      102.
2 B      104.
3 C      106.
4 D      108.

# validate with the full dataset
full_data |> group_by(group) |> summarise(mean = mean(value))

# A tibble: 4 × 2
  group  mean
  <chr> <dbl>
1 A      102.
2 B      104.
3 C      106.
4 D      108.

Not directly.     tibble(chunk_median = median(chunk$value))
}

chunk_medians <- read_csv_chunked(
    file_path,
    callback = DataFrameCallback$new(map_median),
    chunk_size = 1000
)

median(chunk_medians$chunk_median)

[1] 103.9775

median(full_data$value)

[1] 103.99


This is close, but not equal, and nothing tells us how far off it is. title: Lab 10
text:
This lab accompanies the Week 10 notes, Working with Big Data.

Check how big a dataset really is, and read only the part of it you need.
Process a large file in chunks with read_csv_chunked(), using a “map” step and a “reduce” step.
Understand which summaries can be combined exactly across chunks, and which cannot.
See how these methods behave on a larger file, and when chunking pays off.

When you have finished the lab, there are more questions on the same data in lab_10_practice.qmd, including standard deviations from chunks, and using DuckDB to do the work in a database.


The code below generates a large amount of dummy data for you to work with. It has two important parameters:

n: the number of rows
file_path: the path of the file written to

The data file contains four columns:

An id
A timestamp
A group (A, B, C or D)
A (numeric) value



Code
set.seed(2025)

n <- 100000L  # data rows
if (!dir.exists("data")) dir.create("data")
file_path <- paste0("data/large_data_", n, ".csv")  # path to data

generate_data <- function() {
    group <- sample(c("A","B","C","D"), n, replace = TRUE, prob = c(0.4, 0.3, 0.2, 0.1))
    dat <- data.frame(
        id = seq_len(n),
        timestamp = as.POSIXct("2020-01-01", tz = "UTC") + runif(n, 0, 365*24*3600),
        group = group,
        value = rnorm(n, mean = 100, sd = 20) + as.numeric(factor(group, levels = c("A","B","C","D"))) * 2 + rnorm(n, 0, 1)
    )

    dat$value <- round(dat$value, 2)

    readr::write_csv(dat, file_path)
    message("Wrote ", nrow(dat), " rows to ", file_path)
}
if (!file.exists(file_path)) generate_data()


Wrote 100000 rows to data/large_data_100000.csv








NoteThis isn’t really “big” data



The file has 100,000 rows and is only about 3.5MB. It easily fits in memory, and read_csv() reads it in a fraction of a second. Genuinely big data would be tedious to work with in a short lab, because most of the time would be spent waiting. This data is big enough to give you an idea of how the tools work, but not big enough to be a problem. Task 2 uses a larger file to show what changes.


Before working with the data in chunks, let’s check how big it actually is (see “Is my data actually big?” in the Week 10 notes).

How large is the data file on disk, in MB? (Hint: file.size() gives the size in bytes.)
Read the file into a tibble with read_csv(). How much memory does it use? How does this compare with the size of the file?
Now read only the group and value columns. How does the memory used change?
Read only the first 1000 rows. When might this be useful, and what is the risk?
Do you need the tools in the rest of this lab for this data?


Solution. The file is about 3.5MB.

library(tidyverse)

Warning: package 'dplyr' was built under R version 4.4.3

file.size(file_path) / 1e6

[1] 3.534499


Once it is loaded into a tibble, the data take up about the same amount of memory as the file does on disk. The size on disk is a rough guide to the memory needed.

full_data <- read_csv(file_path)
format(object.size(full_data), units = "MB")

[1] "3.1 Mb"


Reading only the two columns we need uses roughly half the memory, because we no longer store id and timestamp. This can make a big difference if a file has many columns but the analysis uses only a few.

two_columns <- read_csv(file_path, col_select = c(group, value))
format(object.size(two_columns), units = "MB")

[1] "1.5 Mb"


n_max reads only the first rows, which is useful for writing and testing code quickly before running it on the whole file. The risk is that the first rows may not be representative of the rest: for example, if the file were sorted by group, we would see only group A. Here the rows are in a random order, so the first 1000 rows happen to be representative, with the groups in roughly the proportions of the whole file.

# A tibble: 4 × 2
  group     n
  <chr> <int>
1 A       384
2 B       305
3 C       204
4 D       107


For this data, no. The whole file fits in memory many times over and loads in a fraction of a second, so read_csv() would be the right tool. We use chunks here to learn how they work; they pay off only when the data are too big to load.

# Load required libraries
library(tidyverse)

# Define a callback function to process each chunk
process_chunk <- function(chunk, pos) {
  chunk |>
    summarize(chunk_sum = sum(value, na.rm = TRUE)) |>
    pull()
}

# This performs the "map" step.
chunk_results <- read_csv_chunked(
  file_path,
  callback = DataFrameCallback$new(process_chunk),
  chunk_size = 1000
)


── Column specification ────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
cols(
  id = col_double(),
  timestamp = col_datetime(format = ""),
  group = col_character(),
  value = col_double()
)

end.time <- Sys.time()
print(paste0("It took ", end.time - start.time, " seconds"))

[1] "It took 0.0807700157165527 seconds"

What is the sum of value for group A?
What are the sums of value for each group? (Hint: try to write the map first, and check what it returns. Then think about the best way to perform the Reduce. You can do it with the reduce function, but you don’t need to!)

100000

Very small chunks are slow: with chunk_size = 10 the callback is called 10,000 times, and each call has a fixed cost (setting up the chunk, running the function, storing the result) that has nothing to do with how much data is in the chunk. title: Lab 7 Practice Questions
text:
These questions are for extra practice after Lab 7, using the same LEGO database. Tasks 1–3 follow on from Task 1 of the lab (reading SQL and the database schema), and Tasks 4–6 from Task 2 of the lab (dbplyr). Questions marked Extension are more challenging.
As in the lab, you are not expected to write SQL yourself: you will read SQL queries in Tasks 1–3, and write dplyr code in Tasks 4–6. The schema of the database is shown in downloads_schema.png, and in the lab.
The cell below connects to the database and creates the lazy tables used in Tasks 4–6.

library(DBI)
library(tidyverse)

Warning: package 'dplyr' was built under R version 4.4.3

con <- dbConnect(RSQLite::SQLite(), "data/lego.sqlite")

Write down the question that each query answers. Which query filters individual sets, and which filters whole years?


Solution. Query C answers for each year, how many sets with at least 1,000 parts were released? WHERE is evaluated before GROUP BY, so it removes the smaller sets first, and the remaining large sets are then counted by year. Years with no large sets do not appear at all, so the result starts in 1985.
Query D answers in which years were at least 500 sets released, and how many? HAVING is evaluated after GROUP BY, so it keeps or removes whole years, based on the number of sets in each: only 2011–2016 pass.

A colleague wants to know how many sets there are in every theme, including any themes with no sets. They have tried three queries, each of which lists the five themes with the fewest sets.

Solution. Query E uses an inner JOIN, which keeps only the themes that match at least one set. A theme with no sets, such as Race, disappears from the result altogether, so the smallest count in Query E is 1.
Query F uses a LEFT JOIN, which keeps every theme. A theme with no sets is kept as a single row, with NULL in all of the columns from sets. But COUNT(*) counts rows, including that one, so Race is reported as having 1 set, just like Castle (id 25), which really does have one.
Query G also uses a LEFT JOIN, but COUNT(sets.set_num) counts only the rows in which set_num is not NULL, so Race correctly has 0 sets. Query G is the one your colleague wants.

Solution. The first query answers which themes have no sets? The subquery lists the theme_id of every set, and the outer query keeps the themes whose id is not in that list. These are exactly the themes with n_sets equal to 0 in Query G; there are 39 of them.
The second query counts the themes that have no sets of their own (the first condition) and are the parent of at least one other theme (the second condition): 13 of the 39. For these themes, the sets are recorded under their sub-themes instead. The other 26 themes have no sets in this database at all.




This task follows on from the CREATE TABLE question in Task 1 of the lab. Here are the statements that were used to create three more of the tables.
CREATE TABLE themes (
    id INTEGER,
    name TEXT,
    parent_id INTEGER,
    PRIMARY KEY (id)
);

CREATE TABLE sets (
    set_num TEXT,
    name TEXT,
    year INTEGER,
    theme_id INTEGER,
    num_parts INTEGER,
    PRIMARY KEY (set_num),
    FOREIGN KEY (theme_id) REFERENCES themes(id)
);

CREATE TABLE colors (
    id INTEGER,
    name TEXT,
    rgb TEXT,
    is_trans TEXT,
    PRIMARY KEY (id)
);

What does themes.parent_id refer to? What kind of relationship is this? What is missing from the CREATE TABLE statement for themes?
Use the queries below to see what values colors.is_trans and inventory_parts.is_spare contain. Which column type would have been a better choice?


SELECT is_trans, COUNT(*) AS n_colours
FROM colors
GROUP BY is_trans;


2 records


is_trans
n_colours




f
107


t
28






SELECT is_spare, COUNT(*) AS n_rows
FROM inventory_parts
GROUP BY is_spare;


2 records


is_spare
n_rows




f
550574


t
29495






Solution. parent_id refers to the id of another row of the same table: for example, theme 220 (City) has parent 217 (Advent Sub-Set). This is a one-to-many relationship between themes and itself: one parent theme can have many sub-themes, but each theme has at most one parent. The schema figure in the lab does not show it.
The statement for themes declares no FOREIGN KEY (parent_id) REFERENCES themes(id), so nothing records that the two columns are linked, and a database that checks foreign keys could not stop a theme from having a parent that does not exist.
Both is_trans and is_spare hold the text 't' or 'f'. A BOOLEAN column would say what the columns mean and, in a database that checks types, stop other values (such as 'yes' or 'T') from creeping in. (SQLite is less strict about both types and foreign keys than most databases: see Using SQLite in the Week 7 notes.)




This task follows on from Task 1 of the lab, but uses a different database. A small library has designed the database below, to record its members, its books and its loans.
CREATE TABLE members (
    member_id INTEGER,
    name TEXT,
    email TEXT,
    date_of_birth TEXT,
    PRIMARY KEY (member_id)
);

CREATE TABLE books (
    isbn TEXT,
    title TEXT,
    authors TEXT,  -- for example 'Wickham, H.; Grolemund, G.'
    year_published TEXT,
    price TEXT
);

CREATE TABLE loans (
    loan_id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY AUTOINCREMENT,
    member_id INTEGER,
    member_name TEXT,
    isbn TEXT,
    date_borrowed DATE,
    date_returned DATE,
    FOREIGN KEY (member_id) REFERENCES members(member_id)
);

Find as many problems with this design as you can. For each one, say what could go wrong.
How would you store the authors of each book instead? What kind of relationship is there between books and authors?
Which columns hold personal data? Which of them does the library need, and who should be able to see them?
Extension: Write corrected CREATE TABLE statements.


Solution. There are several problems:

books has no primary key. The same book could be entered twice, and there is no way to identify a single book. isbn is a natural choice of key.
loans.isbn is not a foreign key. A loan could refer to a book that the library does not have. (It cannot be a foreign key at the moment, because a foreign key must refer to a primary key, and books does not have one.)
Wrong column types. year_published should be an INTEGER, price a REAL and date_of_birth a DATE. Stored as text, they cannot be sorted or compared correctly (as text, '9.99' sorts after '10.50'), and nothing stops values such as 'about 2010' from being entered.
loans.member_name repeats members.name. The name is stored again for every loan, and if a member changes their name, the two tables will disagree. It can always be found by joining loans to members, so it should be removed.
email is not UNIQUE. Two members could be registered with the same email address, which is probably a mistake (or the same person registered twice).
Copies. A library often has several copies of the same book, but a loan only records the ISBN, so we cannot tell which copy is on loan, or how many copies are available.

authors holds a list of names in a single column, which is not tidy (see the Week 4 notes): to find all the books by one author, we would have to search inside the text of every row. Books and authors are in a many-to-many relationship: a book can have several authors, and an author can write several books. As we saw for sets and parts in the lab, this needs an authors table, with one row per author, and a linking table book_authors, with one row for each author of each book.
name, email and date_of_birth are personal data, and are subject to data protection law (see the Week 7 notes and Data Ethics). The library needs a way to contact its members, but it is not clear that it needs their date of birth (unless, for example, children’s membership works differently), and it should not collect data it does not need. Staff issuing books need to see names; an analyst studying which books are popular needs none of these columns, and could be given only summaries.
For the extension, one possible design is:
CREATE TABLE members (
    member_id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY AUTOINCREMENT,
    name TEXT,
    email TEXT UNIQUE
);

CREATE TABLE books (
    isbn TEXT PRIMARY KEY,
    title TEXT,
    year_published INTEGER,
    price REAL
);

CREATE TABLE authors (
    author_id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY AUTOINCREMENT,
    name TEXT
);

CREATE TABLE book_authors (
    isbn TEXT,
    author_id INTEGER,
    PRIMARY KEY (isbn, author_id),
    FOREIGN KEY (isbn) REFERENCES books(isbn),
    FOREIGN KEY (author_id) REFERENCES authors(author_id)
);

CREATE TABLE copies (
    copy_id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY AUTOINCREMENT,
    isbn TEXT,
    FOREIGN KEY (isbn) REFERENCES books(isbn)
);

CREATE TABLE loans (
    loan_id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY AUTOINCREMENT,
    member_id INTEGER,
    copy_id INTEGER,
    date_borrowed DATE,
    date_returned DATE,  -- NULL if the copy has not been returned yet
    FOREIGN KEY (member_id) REFERENCES members(member_id),
    FOREIGN KEY (copy_id) REFERENCES copies(copy_id)
);
The primary key of book_authors combines both of its columns, like the key of inventory_parts in the lab: each pair of book and author should appear once.




This task follows on from Task 2 of the lab.

Write dplyr code that answers the same question as Query B from Task 1 of the lab, which counts the sets for each theme name. Use show_query() to compare the SQL that dbplyr generates with Query B. (Hint: what happens to the two name columns when you join sets to themes?)


Solution. Both sets and themes have a column called name, so a join gives two columns, name.x and name.y (see the Week 5 notes). Selecting and renaming the columns we need from themes first avoids this:

sets_by_theme_name <- sets |>
    inner_join(
        themes |> select(id, theme_name = name),
        by = c("theme_id" = "id")
    ) |>
    group_by(theme_name) |>
    summarise(n_sets = n(), .groups = "drop") |>
    arrange(desc(n_sets)) |>
    head(5)

show_query(sets_by_theme_name)

<SQL>
SELECT `theme_name`, COUNT(*) AS `n_sets`
FROM (
  SELECT `sets`.*, `themes`.`name` AS `theme_name`
  FROM `sets`
  INNER JOIN `themes`
    ON (`sets`.`theme_id` = `themes`.`id`)
) AS `q01`
GROUP BY `theme_name`
ORDER BY `n_sets` DESC
LIMIT 5

collect(sets_by_theme_name)

# A tibble: 5 × 2
  theme_name   n_sets
  <chr>         <int>
1 Supplemental    496
2 Technic         435
3 City            287
4 Friends         269
5 Basic Set       257


The generated SQL does the join in a subquery, and then groups its result, but it gives the same answer as Query B.

In the lab, we counted the total number of parts of each colour, in the database:

inventory_parts |>
    group_by(color_id) |>
    summarise(total = sum(quantity, na.rm = TRUE), .groups = "drop") |>
    collect()


Extend this pipeline to find the names of the five most common colours. Do as much of the work as possible in the database.
Does your answer include spare parts? Change your code so that it doesn’t. Does the answer change?


Solution. The join to colors, the sorting and the head() can all be done in the database, so only five rows are sent to R:

inventory_parts |>
    group_by(color_id) |>
    summarise(total = sum(quantity, na.rm = TRUE), .groups = "drop") |>
    inner_join(colors, by = c("color_id" = "id")) |>
    arrange(desc(total)) |>
    head(5) |>
    collect()

# A tibble: 5 × 5
  color_id  total name              rgb    is_trans
     <int>  <int> <chr>             <chr>  <chr>   
1        0 396416 Black             05131D f       
2       15 221553 White             FFFFFF f       
3       71 201858 Light Bluish Gray A0A5A9 f       
4        4 169983 Red               C91A09 f       
5       72 148584 Dark Bluish Gray  6C6E68 f       


This includes spare parts. To leave them out, we filter on is_spare, which holds the text 'f' for parts that are not spares:

inventory_parts |>
    filter(is_spare == "f") |>
    group_by(color_id) |>
    summarise(total = sum(quantity, na.rm = TRUE), .groups = "drop") |>
    inner_join(colors, by = c("color_id" = "id")) |>
    arrange(desc(total)) |>
    head(5) |>
    collect()

# A tibble: 5 × 5
  color_id  total name              rgb    is_trans
     <int>  <int> <chr>             <chr>  <chr>   
1        0 390863 Black             05131D f       
2       15 218931 White             FFFFFF f       
3       71 197244 Light Bluish Gray A0A5A9 f       
4        4 168029 Red               C91A09 f       
5       72 146603 Dark Bluish Gray  6C6E68 f       


The totals fall, but the five most common colours, and their order, stay the same.

A friend is interested in three themes, which they have stored in a tibble:

chosen <- tibble(name = c("Star Wars", "Harry Potter", "Ninjago"))


Try joining themes to chosen. What happens, and how can you fix it?
Count the number of sets in each of the three chosen themes. How many rows of themes matched each name? Does your count for Star Wars include every Star Wars set?


Solution. themes is a table in the database, but chosen is a tibble in R, so the join fails:

themes |> inner_join(chosen, by = "name")

Error in `auto_copy()`:
! `x` and `y` must share the same src.
ℹ `x` is a <tbl_SQLiteConnection/tbl_dbi/tbl_sql/tbl_lazy/tbl> object.
ℹ `y` is a <tbl_df/tbl/data.frame> object.
ℹ Set `copy = TRUE` if `y` can be copied to the same source as `x` (may be
  slow).


As in the Week 7 notes, copy = TRUE copies chosen into a temporary table in the database, so that the join can run there:

themes |>
    inner_join(chosen, by = "name", copy = TRUE) |>
    collect()

# A tibble: 8 × 3
     id name         parent_id
  <int> <chr>            <int>
1    18 Star Wars            1
2   158 Star Wars           NA
3   209 Star Wars          207
4   225 Star Wars          217
5   261 Star Wars          258
6   431 Star Wars          425
7   246 Harry Potter        NA
8   435 Ninjago             NA


Six different themes are called Star Wars, while Harry Potter and Ninjago match one theme each. To count the sets, we join the matching themes to sets:

themes |>
    inner_join(chosen, by = "name", copy = TRUE) |>
    select(theme_id = id, theme_name = name) |>
    inner_join(sets, by = "theme_id") |>
    count(theme_name) |>
    collect()

# A tibble: 3 × 2
  theme_name       n
  <chr>        <int>
1 Harry Potter    26
2 Ninjago        191
3 Star Wars      211


This counts the sets in all six themes called Star Wars, but not the sets in sub-themes of Star Wars that have other names, so it misses many Star Wars sets. Task 5 groups the sub-themes together.




This task combines both tasks of the lab. In the lab, we found that counting sets by theme gives a misleading picture of which themes are the most popular, partly because large themes are split into many sub-themes.

Count the sets in each theme family: a theme together with all of its sub-themes. For now, assume that a family is a theme with no parent, together with the themes whose parent it is. (Hint: you can join themes to itself. if_else() from the Week 2 notes is also useful.)
Which families have the most sets? What would you now conclude about the most popular theme, and how confident are you?
Extension: Your answer probably includes Advent Sub-Set, but this theme itself has a parent. How deep does the nesting of themes go? Count the sets in each top-level theme, which has no parent.


Solution. For each theme, we look up its parent by joining themes to a copy of itself. Its family is its parent, if it has one, and otherwise the theme itself:

theme_family <- themes |>
    select(theme_id = id, parent_id) |>
    mutate(family_id = if_else(is.na(parent_id), theme_id, parent_id))

sets |>
    inner_join(theme_family, by = "theme_id") |>
    count(family_id) |>
    inner_join(themes |> select(family_id = id, family = name), by = "family_id") |>
    arrange(desc(n)) |>
    head(6) |>
    collect()

# A tibble: 6 × 3
  family_id     n family                 
      <int> <int> <chr>                  
1       217   625 Advent Sub-Set         
2       158   538 Star Wars              
3       443   455 Service Packs          
4       465   441 Universal Building Set 
5       535   441 Collectible Minifigures
6       501   433 Gear                   


We count by family_id rather than by name, because names are not unique, and only then join themes to itself to look up each family’s name.
Advent Sub-Set is a family of advent calendars, in which each day counts as a set, and Service Packs are spare parts, so the count of sets is still a poor measure of popularity. Star Wars, with over 500 sets, is the largest family of building sets here. We should not be very confident in any ranking, though: the counts measure how many products were released, not how many were sold, they depend on how the themes in the database have been organised, and the database contains no sales data at all.
For the extension, we join each theme to its parent and its grandparent, and check whether any grandparent has a parent of its own:

theme_levels <- themes |>
    select(theme_id = id, parent_id) |>
    left_join(
        themes |> select(parent_id = id, grandparent_id = parent_id),
        by = "parent_id"
    ) |>
    left_join(
        themes |> select(grandparent_id = id, great_grandparent_id = parent_id),
        by = "grandparent_id"
    )

theme_levels |>
    summarise(
        n_with_parent = sum(!is.na(parent_id), na.rm = TRUE),
        n_with_grandparent = sum(!is.na(grandparent_id), na.rm = TRUE),
        n_with_great_grandparent = sum(!is.na(great_grandparent_id), na.rm = TRUE)
    ) |>
    collect()

# A tibble: 1 × 3
  n_with_parent n_with_grandparent n_with_great_grandparent
          <int>              <int>                    <int>
1           503                156                        0


Some themes have a grandparent, but none has a great-grandparent, so themes are nested at most three levels deep. A theme’s top-level theme is therefore its grandparent if it has one, otherwise its parent if it has one, and otherwise the theme itself:

sets |>
    inner_join(theme_levels, by = "theme_id") |>
    mutate(
        top_id = case_when(
            !is.na(grandparent_id) ~ grandparent_id,
            !is.na(parent_id) ~ parent_id,
            TRUE ~ theme_id
        )
    ) |>
    count(top_id) |>
    inner_join(themes |> select(top_id = id, top_theme = name), by = "top_id") |>
    arrange(desc(n)) |>
    head(6) |>
    collect()

# A tibble: 6 × 3
  top_id     n top_theme             
   <int> <int> <chr>                 
1     50  1098 Town                  
2    206   923 Seasonal              
3    158   592 Star Wars             
4      1   533 Technic               
5    443   456 Service Packs         
6    465   441 Universal Building Set


At the top level, Town (which includes City) has the most sets, and the advent calendars are now counted under Seasonal.




This task follows on from Task 2 of the lab.

Extension: Each set has a num_parts column, but its parts are also listed in inventory_parts. For how many sets do the two agree? (Hint: think about what we found in Task 1 of the lab about spare parts and inventory versions.) What can you say about the sets for which they disagree?


Solution. First, we add up the quantities in each set’s inventories, and compare the total with num_parts:

inventory_parts |>
    inner_join(inventories, by = c("inventory_id" = "id")) |>
    group_by(set_num) |>
    summarise(total = sum(quantity, na.rm = TRUE), .groups = "drop") |>
    inner_join(sets, by = "set_num") |>
    summarise(
        n_sets = n(),
        n_agree = sum(total == num_parts, na.rm = TRUE)
    ) |>
    collect()

# A tibble: 1 × 2
  n_sets n_agree
   <int>   <int>
1  10713    5811


Only about half agree. This total includes spare parts, which are not counted in num_parts. Leaving them out makes a big difference:

inventory_parts |>
    filter(is_spare == "f") |>
    inner_join(inventories, by = c("inventory_id" = "id")) |>
    group_by(set_num) |>
    summarise(total = sum(quantity, na.rm = TRUE), .groups = "drop") |>
    inner_join(sets, by = "set_num") |>
    summarise(
        n_sets = n(),
        n_agree = sum(total == num_parts, na.rm = TRUE)
    ) |>
    collect()

# A tibble: 1 × 2
  n_sets n_agree
   <int>   <int>
1  10710   10479


The total also adds up every inventory of a set, so a set with several inventory versions is counted several times. Keeping only the first version of each inventory removes this:

part_totals <- inventory_parts |>
    filter(is_spare == "f") |>
    inner_join(
        inventories |> filter(version == 1),
        by = c("inventory_id" = "id")
    ) |>
    group_by(set_num, inventory_id) |>
    summarise(total = sum(quantity, na.rm = TRUE), .groups = "drop") |>
    inner_join(sets, by = "set_num")

part_totals |>
    summarise(
        n_sets = n(),
        n_agree = sum(total == num_parts, na.rm = TRUE),
        n_fewer = sum(total < num_parts, na.rm = TRUE)
    ) |>
    collect()

# A tibble: 1 × 3
  n_sets n_agree n_fewer
   <int>   <int>   <int>
1  10709   10486     223


Now almost all of the sets agree. For every set that disagrees, the inventory lists fewer parts than num_parts. Some of these are sets that contain other sets, such as advent calendars, whose parts are listed in the inventories of the sets they contain (through inventory_sets), rather than in their own:

part_totals |>
    filter(total < num_parts) |>
    semi_join(inventory_sets, by = "inventory_id") |>
    count() |>
    collect()

# A tibble: 1 × 1
      n
  <int>
1    47


For the rest, the data do not tell us why the totals differ; most differ by only a few parts.

We have finished with the database, so we close the connection:

dbDisconnect(con)

text:
These questions are for extra practice after Lab 7, using the same LEGO database. Tasks 1–3 follow on from Task 1 of the lab (reading SQL and the database schema), and Tasks 4–6 from Task 2 of the lab (dbplyr). Questions marked Extension are more challenging.

Solution. Query E uses an inner JOIN, which keeps only the themes that match at least one set. A theme with no sets, such as Race, disappears from the result altogether, so the smallest count in Query E is 1.
Query F uses a LEFT JOIN, which keeps every theme. A theme with no sets is kept as a single row, with NULL in all of the columns from sets. But COUNT(*) counts rows, including that one, so Race is reported as having 1 set, just like Castle (id 25), which really does have one.
